options.A: Patents guarantee adoption because legal rights replace market fit
options.B: Patents eliminate rivalry because substitutes become illegal forever
options.C: Patents grant rights but disclosure can accelerate rival learning
options.D: Patents prevent learning because rivals cannot read patents legally

2yr-13.explanation: Patents can be double-edged: monopoly rights plus disclosure-driven learning.

2yr-13.stem: A press release announces a “revolutionary” concept without a working artifact. The correct label is:

options.A: Innovation because communication equals commercialization
options.B: Imitation because all concepts copy prior work
options.C: Idea, not invention or innovation yet
options.D: Invention because announcing makes it real

2yr-13.explanation: Idea is conceptual; invention needs a working artifact; innovation needs market launch.

2yr-13.stem: A rival copies Netflix’s ad-tier interface but lacks targeting data and experimentation routines. Best inference is:

options.A: Feature imitation always wins because followers avoid early mistakes
options.B: Feature imitation is blocked because ad tiers are patent-protected
options.C: Feature imitation is sufficient because customers see the same tier
options.D: Feature imitation is incomplete without replicating capability systems

2yr-13.explanation: Outcomes depend on underlying learning routines and data assets, not surface features.

2yr-13.stem: A startup says “imitation proves we are losing.” Chapter 7 implies instead:

options.A: Imitation often follows success; the issue becomes renewal
options.B: Imitation is impossible in software markets
options.C: Imitation occurs only after failure, not success
options.D: Imitation occurs only in maturity, not early stages

2yr-13.explanation: Copying can signal success; strategic focus shifts to sustaining advantage.

2yr-13.stem: A startup says “we innovated” because we filed a patent, yet have zero customers. The sharp correction is:

options.A: Innovation requires commercialization and adoption, not filings
options.B: Innovation is identical to invention, so filing is enough
options.C: Patents are innovation because courts validate market demand
options.D: Innovation equals imitation because followers define standards

2yr-13.explanation: Innovation is commercialization; patents alone do not create adoption.

2yr-13.stem: A startup’s edge is a short-lived ranking algorithm in a fast-cycle market. Best appropriability stance is:

options.A: Wait for maturity because early markets punish secrecy
options.B: Broad patents because disclosure prevents competitor learning
options.C: Secrecy and process embedding when enforcement lags market tempo
options.D: No protection because appropriability never matters in tech

2yr-13.explanation: When markets move faster than legal enforcement, secrecy and execution can dominate.

2yr-13.stem: A successful feature is copied within weeks. The most Chapter 7–consistent inference is:

options.A: Imitation follows success; sustain advantage via continuous innovation
options.B: Copying is illegal by default in digital markets
options.C: Copying proves failure; exit because advantage is impossible
options.D: Copying implies radical innovation and permanent monopoly

2yr-13.explanation: In the Four I’s, imitation follows innovation; advantage depends on renewal and complements.

2yr-13.stem: Netflix keeps its recommendation logic unpatented and tightly confidential. This choice best illustrates:

options.A: Patents maximize secrecy and prevent rivals from reading disclosures
options.B: Trade secrets avoid disclosure and preserve algorithmic know-how advantage
options.C: Ideas become innovations once they are published in academic venues
options.D: Imitation reduces risk because followers gain legitimacy through copying

2yr-13.explanation: Patents require disclosure; trade secrets preserve secrecy when disclosure would erase advantage.

2yr-13.stem: Patent expiry followed by entry fits which story best?

options.A: Platform rents replacing patent rents automatically
options.B: Temporary monopoly until imitation/entry accelerates
options.C: Consumer surplus replacing producer capture by definition
options.D: Permanent monopoly because patents never end

2yr-13.explanation: Patents are time-limited; expiry enables easier entry and imitation.

2yr-13.stem: The Four I’s sequence is best captured as:

options.A: Innovation → Imitation → Invention → Idea
options.B: Idea → Innovation → Invention → Imitation
options.C: Idea → Invention → Innovation → Imitation
options.D: Invention → Idea → Imitation → Innovation

2yr-13.explanation: Chapter 7 defines innovation as commercialization after invention, with imitation following success.

2yr-13.stem: The most discriminating test between “invention” and “innovation” is whether:

options.A: Scientists agree it is publishable
options.B: It has a patent number assigned
options.C: Customers adopt it through commercialization at scale
options.D: It uses new technology internally

2yr-13.explanation: Commercialization and adoption are the defining boundary between invention and innovation.

2yr-13.stem: “AI automation may displace routine jobs and shift education returns.” This is tied most to:

options.A: First industrial revolution implications
options.B: Fourth industrial revolution implications
options.C: Third industrial revolution implications
options.D: Second industrial revolution implications

2yr-13.explanation: The fourth industrial revolution emphasizes AI/automation/cyber-physical systems and social impacts.

2yr-13.stem: “Innovation equals invention.” The cleanest rebuttal is:

options.A: Invention is decline; innovation is maturity efficiency
options.B: Invention is imitation; innovation is branding redesign
options.C: Invention is commercialization; innovation is abstract ideation
options.D: Invention is creation; innovation is commercialization and adoption

2yr-13.explanation: Chapter 7 separates invention (artifact) from innovation (commercialization).

2yr-13.stem: A SaaS startup wants to cross the chasm in one vertical before expanding broadly. This is aligned with:

options.A: Decline-stage strategy because chasm crossing is easiest once an industry begins shrinking structurally
options.B: Horizontal strategy to enter all verticals first so early majority can pick any configuration needed
options.C: Laggard-first strategy because laggards are the biggest market and adopt reliably without support
options.D: Beachhead strategy to win one niche with references and whole-product completeness, then expand adjacently

2yr-13.explanation: Chasm crossing favors a focused beachhead to build references and whole product.

2yr-13.stem: A chasm-crossing “beachhead” is mainly used to:

options.A: Target laggards for predictable first adoption
options.B: Create credible references and reduce risk for pragmatists
options.C: Avoid learning and delay commercialization
options.D: Eliminate substitutes through patents

2yr-13.explanation: Beachheads create references and whole-product completeness to reduce pragmatist risk.

2yr-13.stem: A company markets heavily to late majority before fixing early majority concerns. Most likely result:

options.A: Strong adoption, because late majority buys without references, standards, or support
options.B: Weak adoption only if patents exist, because patents make late-majority buyers suspicious
options.C: Weak adoption, because late majority waits for entrenched standards and strong brands built via early majority momentum
options.D: Strong adoption, because late majority values beta testing and tolerates imperfections most

2yr-13.explanation: Late majority generally follows early majority adoption and wants established standards and brands.

2yr-13.stem: A fintech category sees rapid adoption, strong new user growth, and many entrants adding capacity. Stage inference is:

options.A: Decline stage, where demand falls structurally and new entrants avoid the market entirely
options.B: Maturity stage, where replacement dominates and firms compete mainly on incremental efficiency
options.C: Growth stage, where adoption accelerates and entry intensifies as firms pursue scale and position
options.D: Shakeout stage, where exits dominate because consolidation has already reduced competitors

2yr-13.explanation: Growth is rapid adoption plus entry; shakeout is consolidation and exits.

2yr-13.stem: A firm in growth should typically prioritize:

options.A: Harvesting cash immediately
options.B: Eliminating variety to enforce standards
options.C: Scaling while learning and positioning before consolidation arrives
options.D: Exiting early to avoid rivalry

2yr-13.explanation: Growth rewards scaling and positioning; harvest strategies fit later stages.

2yr-13.stem: A firm in introduction stage should typically prioritize:

options.A: Learning fast and finding product–market fit under uncertainty
options.B: Locking standards through scale manufacturing
options.C: Harvesting stable cash flows
options.D: Consolidating competitors

2yr-13.explanation: Introduction is uncertain; learning and early adoption dominate.

2yr-13.stem: A firm tries to cross the chasm by adding features while reliability and support remain weak. The most likely outcome is:

options.A: It succeeds because pragmatists adopt first and prefer novelty even when service is unreliable
options.B: It fails only if patents expire because chasm crossing is mainly a legal exclusivity problem
options.C: It succeeds because features substitute fully for standards, references, and after-sales support
options.D: It still fails because early majority values risk reduction and whole-product support over feature novelty

2yr-13.explanation: Pragmatists value risk reduction and whole-product completeness.

2yr-13.stem: A market shows dominant design, intense rivalry, and exits. Best stage label:

options.A: Growth
options.B: Decline
options.C: Introduction
options.D: Shakeout

2yr-13.explanation: Shakeout features consolidation and exits around a dominant design.

2yr-13.stem: A market shows intense consolidation, exits, and a few surviving leaders around a dominant design. Stage inference is:

options.A: Shakeout stage, where rivalry rises and weaker firms exit as the industry consolidates
options.B: Decline stage, where demand is near zero and firms cannot profitably sell any units
options.C: Introduction stage, where uncertainty falls and designs become more diverse with stable entry
options.D: Growth stage, where entry is high and exits are low because demand is exploding everywhere

2yr-13.explanation: Shakeout is defined by consolidation: rivalry, exits, fewer survivors.

2yr-13.stem: A market shows saturation, slower growth, and competition shifting to incremental improvements and efficiency. Stage inference is:

options.A: Maturity stage, where growth slows and firms compete through efficiency and incremental innovation
options.B: Growth stage, where adoption accelerates and variety expands faster than efficiency pressures
options.C: Shakeout stage, where exits dominate and only a few firms remain after consolidation
options.D: Introduction stage, where uncertainty is highest and designs compete before standards emerge

2yr-13.explanation: Maturity: slower growth, saturation, incremental improvement, efficiency focus.

2yr-13.stem: A micro-mobility industry saw rapid entry and then many exits in several cities. This pattern most closely signals:

options.A: Decline stage completion, where demand collapses to near zero and no replacement cycles remain
options.B: Shakeout stage dynamics, where rivalry intensifies, weaker firms exit, and consolidation accelerates
options.C: Introduction stage stability, where uncertainty drops and competitors converge without exits
options.D: Maturity stage expansion, where entrants proliferate and product variety grows without consolidation

2yr-13.explanation: Shakeout is the consolidation phase after growth, with rising rivalry and exits.

2yr-13.stem: A new consumer device market shows explosive demand growth and many entrants, but standards begin to stabilize. This best fits:

options.A: Shakeout stage, where exits dominate because growth has ended and consolidation is underway
options.B: Decline stage, where demand falls structurally and firms should harvest rather than invest
options.C: Growth stage, where adoption accelerates and entry intensifies while standards start to clarify
options.D: Maturity stage, where replacement dominates and innovation becomes mostly incremental efficiency

2yr-13.explanation: Growth features rapid adoption and entry; standards begin stabilizing.

2yr-13.stem: A product is adopted only when necessary and buyers avoid new technology for personal or economic reasons. This describes:

options.A: Technology enthusiasts, who wait for entrenched standards and strong brands before buying
options.B: Laggards, who enter late and adopt only when adoption becomes unavoidable in practice
options.C: Early adopters, who pay premiums for beta products to signal status and experiment
options.D: Early majority, who adopt early and tolerate uncertainty because novelty is intrinsically valued

2yr-13.explanation: Laggards adopt last and reluctantly; they are rarely the main growth engine.

2yr-13.stem: A smartphone market is replacement-driven with slower growth and intense price competition. The best stage label is:

options.A: Decline stage, where adoption becomes unnecessary and firms should exit immediately and harvest cash
options.B: Maturity stage, where replacement demand rises and rivalry focuses on efficiency and pricing
options.C: Introduction stage, where uncertainty is highest and standards have not emerged across producers
options.D: Growth stage, where first-time adoption dominates and differentiation expands variety without pressure

2yr-13.explanation: Maturity features replacement demand, slower growth, and stronger price rivalry.

2yr-13.stem: A wearable category is still searching for a dominant design and has uncertain standards. The most consistent life-cycle stage is:

options.A: Maturity stage, where standards are entrenched and incremental efficiency becomes the main driver
options.B: Decline stage, where the market contracts and firms harvest rather than invest in new designs
options.C: Introduction stage, where uncertainty is high and designs compete before a dominant design emerges
options.D: Shakeout stage, where dominant design is fully settled and entry accelerates without exits

2yr-13.explanation: Introduction features high uncertainty and competing designs; dominant design tends to emerge later.

2yr-13.stem: A “whole product” emphasis means:

options.A: Price cuts alone with no service investment
options.B: Core product alone with maximum features
options.C: Patent portfolio plus PR campaigns
options.D: Core product plus complements, support, reliability, and standards

2yr-13.explanation: Whole product includes ecosystem elements needed to reduce adoption risk for pragmatists.

2yr-13.stem: An EV startup wins early adopters but loses early majority because repairs take months and service is inconsistent. The best diagnosis is:

options.A: It failed the novelty test, where pragmatists demand unproven experimental features more than reliability
options.B: It failed the ‘whole product’ test, where pragmatists need dependable after-sales support and reliability
options.C: It failed the patent test, where pragmatists refuse products lacking legal exclusivity protections
options.D: It failed the price test, where pragmatists adopt only when prices rise and signal premium quality

2yr-13.explanation: Early majority adoption requires risk reduction: support, standards, and reliability.

2yr-13.stem: Apple Vision Pro’s early buyers were largely enthusiasts and early adopters. In chasm terms, the next major hurdle is convincing the:

options.A: Laggards, who pay premium prices for beta products and tolerate high uncertainty in use
options.B: Technology enthusiasts, who adopt after standards are entrenched and brands are well established
options.C: Early majority, who demand reliability, clear use cases, standards, and strong support before adoption
options.D: Late majority, who purchase first and then create reference cases for other segments to follow

2yr-13.explanation: The key chasm is early adopters → early majority; pragmatists demand whole-product completeness and risk reduction.

2yr-13.stem: Generative AI copilots spread rapidly across teams, then adoption slows as firms demand governance and safety. This slowdown most resembles movement toward:

options.A: Decline stage, where market contraction is dominant and new adoption is structurally impossible
options.B: Technology enthusiast dominance, where beta instability is rewarded because experimentation is the main objective
options.C: Laggard entry, where adoption happens only in decline stage and therefore requires forced compliance
options.D: Early majority concerns, where standards, integration, and risk controls become prerequisites for broad adoption

2yr-13.explanation: Mainstream diffusion slows until standards, integration, reliability, and support are in place.

2yr-13.stem: In decline, the most coherent general move is often:

options.A: Build capacity aggressively for scale
options.B: Harvest or niche-focus rather than broad expansion
options.C: Ignore cash flows and reinvest heavily
options.D: Maximize variety and experimentation

2yr-13.explanation: Decline often calls for harvest/consolidation/niche focus, not broad growth investment.

2yr-13.stem: In maturity, competitive advantage often shifts toward:

options.A: Ignoring customer support and complements
options.B: Incremental innovation and efficiency improvements
options.C: Pure monopoly pricing without value improvements
options.D: Radical category creation only

2yr-13.explanation: Maturity competition often centers on incremental improvements and efficiency.

2yr-13.stem: Late majority is similar to early majority but more risk-averse. The most correct statement is:

options.A: Late majority is similar to early majority but more risk-averse and more brand-dependent in adoption
options.B: Late majority is less risk-averse than early adopters and therefore buys unfinished beta designs first
options.C: Late majority is identical to laggards, so both segments should be pursued aggressively for growth
options.D: Late majority buys mainly for novelty, making standards and support far less important than features

2yr-13.explanation: Late majority prefers established standards and brands, and needs strong support.

2yr-13.stem: Smartphones are in growth in many emerging economies and in maturity in developed economies. The clearest implication is:

options.A: The industry life cycle is invalid because a product cannot be in two stages at the same time
options.B: The shakeout stage is irrelevant because digital goods do not experience consolidation dynamics
options.C: The same firm may need different strategies across geographies because life-cycle stage differs by market
options.D: The decline stage must be next everywhere because maturity in one market forces global contraction

2yr-13.explanation: Life-cycle stages can differ by geography; strategy should adapt accordingly.

2yr-13.stem: Tesla’s Model 3/Model Y are discussed as helping it cross the big chasm. The strategic logic is most directly:

options.A: New patents prevent imitation, pushing adoption from laggards toward early enthusiasts immediately
options.B: Higher-priced models create exclusivity, pushing adoption from late majority toward early adopters
options.C: Network effects guarantee adoption, pushing adoption from early majority toward early adopters over time
options.D: Lower-priced models broaden adoption from early adopters toward the early majority segment

2yr-13.explanation: Lower-priced models expand reachable segments and support mainstream diffusion.

2yr-13.stem: The largest “chasm” is typically between:

options.A: Early majority and laggards
options.B: Technology enthusiasts and laggards
options.C: Late majority and laggards
options.D: Early adopters and early majority

2yr-13.explanation: The major chasm is early adopters → early majority (visionaries → pragmatists).

2yr-13.stem: A cheaper, initially inferior product starts in a fringe segment and later improves to threaten incumbents. The closest label is:

options.A: Disruptive innovation, entering from fringe markets and moving upmarket over time to challenge leaders
options.B: Architectural innovation, applying new technology in existing markets without changing market trajectories
options.C: Incremental innovation, improving existing offerings but never threatening incumbent business models
options.D: Radical innovation, beginning as premium performance and targeting mainstream customers from day one

2yr-13.explanation: Disruptive innovations often begin in fringe/new markets and later move upmarket.

2yr-13.stem: A company builds a new chip architecture but sells it to existing data-center customers. Exhibit 7.12 implies:

options.A: Disruptive innovation, because new chips must start low-end and then move up to mainstream buyers
options.B: Architectural innovation, applying a new technology configuration to an existing market space
options.C: Incremental innovation, because semiconductors only improve steadily without discontinuity by definition
options.D: Radical innovation, because any new technology implies a new market regardless of customer base

2yr-13.explanation: New tech applied to existing markets is architectural innovation.

2yr-13.stem: A firm recombines existing modules for a better experience without new science in the same market. Best label is:

options.A: Disruptive innovation
options.B: Radical innovation
options.C: Architectural innovation
options.D: Incremental innovation

2yr-13.explanation: Same market + same tech base recombination typically remains incremental.

2yr-13.stem: A firm reconfigures existing components into a new system architecture for its current customer base without new science. The closest label is:

options.A: Architectural innovation, because any internal redesign necessarily creates a new market by definition
options.B: Disruptive innovation, because system redesigns always begin low-end and then displace premium incumbents
options.C: Radical innovation, because recombination always implies a new market and a new technology knowledge base
options.D: Incremental innovation, because it recombines existing knowledge for existing markets without new technology bases

2yr-13.explanation: Recombination within existing markets/tech base is typically incremental.

2yr-13.stem: A firm sells a premium product that improves mainstream performance and calls it disruptive. Best critique is:

options.A: Definitely disruptive because premium implies new market
options.B: Likely sustaining improvement, not classic disruption trajectory
options.C: Not classifiable because disruption depends only on patents
options.D: Definitely disruptive because better performance defines disruption

2yr-13.explanation: Premium sustaining improvements are not the classic disruptive trajectory.

2yr-13.stem: A firm uses existing tech to reach customers previously outside the category. That is most consistent with:

options.A: Architectural innovation
options.B: Incremental innovation
options.C: Disruptive innovation
options.D: Radical innovation

2yr-13.explanation: New market served with existing technology aligns with architectural innovation.

2yr-13.stem: A firm uses new tech to sell to existing customers. That is most consistent with:

options.A: Architectural innovation
options.B: Disruptive innovation
options.C: Incremental innovation
options.D: Radical innovation

2yr-13.explanation: New technology applied to an existing market is architectural innovation.

2yr-13.stem: A firm’s radical breakthrough is followed by many small upgrades. The best interpretation is:

options.A: Radical creates lead; incremental sustains advantage over time
options.B: Radical makes incremental illegal
options.C: Disruption requires only one upgrade cycle
options.D: Incremental makes radical impossible

2yr-13.explanation: Common pattern: radical innovation creates a lead; incremental sustains it.

2yr-13.stem: A new gene-editing therapy creates a new category and new market applications. In Exhibit 7.12, it best fits:

options.A: Disruptive innovation, starting low-end in existing markets and then improving to match incumbents
options.B: Architectural innovation, targeting new markets using existing technologies without new science
options.C: Incremental innovation, improving existing offerings for existing markets using existing technologies
options.D: Radical innovation, targeting new markets by using new technologies from novel knowledge bases

2yr-13.explanation: Radical innovation is new tech plus new market, often creating new industries.

2yr-13.stem: A premium, higher-performance product is called “disruptive.” The best critique is:

options.A: That pattern resembles sustaining improvement; disruption typically enters fringe or new markets first
options.B: That pattern is disruptive by definition, because disruption equals superior performance at launch
options.C: That pattern is architectural by definition, because premium products always target existing markets
options.D: That pattern is radical by definition, because premium implies new market creation automatically

2yr-13.explanation: Disruption is a trajectory and entry pattern, not simply “better and pricier.”

2yr-13.stem: A product based on new materials and methods targets a new application market. Exhibit 7.12 label is:

options.A: Architectural innovation, using existing technologies to create a new market without new knowledge
options.B: Radical innovation, combining new technologies with new markets and sometimes creating new industries
options.C: Incremental innovation, improving existing products for existing markets with existing technologies
options.D: Disruptive innovation, entering existing markets at premium tiers and then moving downmarket

2yr-13.explanation: New tech + new market is radical innovation.

2yr-13.stem: A smartphone maker upgrades camera software and battery management using the same chip platform for current users. Exhibit 7.12 label is:

options.A: Disruptive innovation, starting low-end and then moving upmarket as incumbents overshoot demand
options.B: Incremental innovation, improving existing products in existing markets using existing technologies
options.C: Architectural innovation, creating new markets using existing technologies without altering the product
options.D: Radical innovation, creating new markets because any improvement creates a new category of buyers

2yr-13.explanation: Existing tech + existing market improvements are incremental.

2yr-13.stem: A startup uses existing payment rails but targets newly served segments in a new market. Exhibit 7.12 suggests:

options.A: Disruptive innovation, requiring inferior quality and low price as a necessary condition always
options.B: Radical innovation, requiring new technologies whenever a new segment is targeted at all
options.C: Architectural innovation, using existing technologies to create or serve a new market space
options.D: Incremental innovation, improving existing offerings for existing markets using the same technology

2yr-13.explanation: New market + existing tech aligns with architectural innovation in Exhibit 7.12.

2yr-13.stem: Amazon improves Alexa with better speech recognition using existing ML methods for existing customers. In Exhibit 7.12 terms, this is:

options.A: Incremental innovation, improving an existing offering for existing markets using existing technologies
options.B: Disruptive innovation, entering a new fringe market and later moving upmarket to displace incumbents
options.C: Architectural innovation, creating a new market using existing technologies with no change in use
options.D: Radical innovation, creating a new market using new technologies that replace prior knowledge bases

2yr-13.explanation: Incremental innovation improves existing offerings for existing markets using existing technologies.

2yr-13.stem: An IoT cyber-physical system linking devices and analytics is most associated with:

options.A: The fourth industrial revolution with AI, automation, robotics, and IoT cyber-physical systems
options.B: The second industrial revolution driven by electrification and mass production
options.C: The first industrial revolution driven by steam power and mechanization
options.D: The third industrial revolution driven by computers but not connected cyber-physical systems

2yr-13.explanation: Chapter 7 associates IoT and cyber-physical systems with the fourth industrial revolution.

2yr-13.stem: Disruptive innovation is best described as:

options.A: Entry via fringe/new markets with different attributes, then upmarket movement
options.B: New technology plus new market always
options.C: Immediate domination of mainstream markets through superior premium performance
options.D: Existing technology plus existing market always

2yr-13.explanation: Disruption is about entry footholds and trajectory, not immediate premium superiority.

2yr-13.stem: Existing tech + existing market improvements generally classify as:

options.A: Architectural
options.B: Incremental
options.C: Disruptive
options.D: Radical

2yr-13.explanation: That is the incremental quadrant in the markets–technology framework.

2yr-13.stem: Existing tech + new market generally classify as:

options.A: Incremental
options.B: Radical
options.C: Architectural
options.D: Disruptive

2yr-13.explanation: Existing technologies serving a new market is architectural innovation.

2yr-13.stem: Fourth industrial revolution dynamics are most likely to increase returns to:

options.A: Education and adaptable human capital, because routine tasks are more automatable
options.B: Corporate secrecy, because diffusion becomes impossible once automation expands
options.C: Inventory stockpiles, because scarcity becomes the main source of advantage
options.D: Retail floor space, because foot traffic is the central moat in cyber-physical markets

2yr-13.explanation: As automation rises, the value of adaptable skills and education increases.

2yr-13.stem: New tech + existing market generally classify as:

options.A: Disruptive
options.B: Radical
options.C: Incremental
options.D: Architectural

2yr-13.explanation: New tech applied to an existing market is architectural innovation.

2yr-13.stem: New tech + new market creation generally classify as:

options.A: Radical
options.B: Architectural
options.C: Incremental
options.D: Disruptive

2yr-13.explanation: New technologies aimed at new markets map to radical innovation.

2yr-13.stem: The diagonal pairing in the framework highlights:

options.A: Incremental vs radical, and architectural vs disruptive
options.B: Incremental vs architectural only
options.C: Disruptive vs incremental only
options.D: Radical vs disruptive only

2yr-13.explanation: Two diagonal contrasts: incremental–radical and architectural–disruptive.

2yr-13.stem: The most diagnostic question for classification is:

options.A: Profit margin changes in the first quarter
options.B: Legal disputes and patent filings
options.C: Influencer engagement and brand mentions
options.D: Existing vs new markets, and existing vs new technologies

2yr-13.explanation: The framework is defined by market newness and technology newness.

2yr-13.stem: “Most innovations are radical.” The best correction is:

options.A: Most innovations are incremental, despite attention to breakthroughs
options.B: Most innovations are architectural only
options.C: Most innovations are disruptive, not incremental
options.D: Most innovations are radical because markets demand novelty

2yr-13.explanation: Chapter 7 stresses that incremental innovations dominate in practice.

2yr-13.stem: “New to our firm” does not necessarily mean “radical.” The correct diagnostic is:

options.A: Newness to market and technology axes, not internal novelty
options.B: Patent status and court enforceability
options.C: Marketing excitement and press coverage intensity
options.D: Founder charisma and early funding size

2yr-13.explanation: Classification depends on market newness and technology newness, not internal unfamiliarity.

2yr-13.stem: A creator platform solves chicken-or-egg by guaranteeing buyers for first creators. This is:

options.A: Decline-stage repositioning
options.B: Architectural innovation classification
options.C: Harvesting demand in maturity stage
options.D: Seeding one side to create early proof and transactions

2yr-13.explanation: Seeding generates liquidity and proof that attracts the other side.

2yr-13.stem: A platform adds complements through third parties. Most accurate implication is:

options.A: Less value potential because complements always cannibalize
options.B: Governance becomes unnecessary because complements self-police
options.C: Network effects become irrelevant once complements exist
options.D: More value potential, but governance complexity rises sharply

2yr-13.explanation: Complements expand value but increase rule-setting and enforcement needs.

2yr-13.stem: A platform becomes valuable because more users join, not because unit costs fall. This is:

options.A: Economies of scale, not network effects
options.B: Life-cycle maturity, not platform dynamics
options.C: Network effects, not just economies of scale
options.D: Radical innovation, not platform dynamics

2yr-13.explanation: Network effects are demand-side; scale economies are supply-side.

2yr-13.stem: A platform competitor copies the interface but lacks users. Why does it matter?

options.A: Inventory ownership is the key; users are secondary
options.B: Advertising alone creates value; user counts are irrelevant
options.C: Without critical mass, network effects are weak and value is lower
options.D: Interface copying is illegal so users automatically migrate

2yr-13.explanation: The network is the product; without participation on both sides, value collapses.

2yr-13.stem: A platform lowers take rate to attract more producers, expecting later growth. This is:

options.A: Crossing the chasm by targeting laggards first
options.B: Eliminating substitutes by predatory pricing
options.C: Converting invention into innovation automatically
options.D: Subsidizing one side to ignite participation and network effects

2yr-13.explanation: Subsidies can build critical mass and ignite network effects.

2yr-13.stem: A platform opens APIs for complements but fails to enforce quality rules. Primary risk is:

options.A: Trust collapses; participation falls; network effects weaken
options.B: Patents prevent low-quality participants from joining
options.C: Trust increases automatically through openness
options.D: Complements matter only in late majority stage

2yr-13.explanation: Openness without governance invites adverse selection and erodes trust.

2yr-13.stem: A platform raises take rates aggressively before stabilizing network effects. Risk is:

options.A: Substitutes vanish because users lock in
options.B: Chasm becomes irrelevant because fees imply reliability
options.C: Rivals exit because fees signal quality
options.D: Participation drops and network effects weaken

2yr-13.explanation: Premature monetization can reduce participation before critical mass, weakening network effects.

2yr-13.stem: A platform restricts third-party producers “to stay in control.” Core risk is:

options.A: Chicken-or-egg disappears because restriction forces joining
options.B: Network effects strengthen because fewer producers increases value
options.C: Ecosystem growth slows; network effects fail to scale
options.D: Chasm crossing becomes automatic because closure signals reliability

2yr-13.explanation: Restriction can throttle variety and participation, weakening network effects.

2yr-13.stem: A platform stagnates after trust scandals. Best explanation is:

options.A: Trust scandals push adoption to late majority faster
options.B: Trust scandals prove radical innovation is occurring
options.C: Reduced participation weakens network effects and value for remaining users
options.D: Trust scandals reduce costs and improve margins

2yr-13.explanation: Participation shocks can trigger negative spirals in network-effect markets.

2yr-13.stem: A platform’s feedback loops create advantage mainly by:

options.A: Eliminating the need for governance and moderation
options.B: Making patents unnecessary for all industries
options.C: Replacing the need for supply-side growth
options.D: Improving match quality and reducing friction through data learning

2yr-13.explanation: Platforms learn from interactions; better matching improves value creation.

2yr-13.stem: A platform’s governance is best seen as:

options.A: A substitute for product design and customer experience
options.B: A late-stage activity only after maturity arrives
options.C: A compliance detail unrelated to platform economics
options.D: A strategic lever shaping value creation and participation quality

2yr-13.explanation: Governance shapes trust and participation—core to platform advantage.

2yr-13.stem: A platform’s “product” includes:

options.A: Only the HR hiring system
options.B: Rules, trust mechanisms, incentives, and matching infrastructure
options.C: Only the user interface and brand slogan
options.D: Only the financing structure and capital policy

2yr-13.explanation: Platform strategy is ecosystem design: roles, incentives, governance, and matching.

2yr-13.stem: A rider becomes a driver within the same platform. This is:

options.A: Architectural innovation
options.B: Multi-homing
options.C: Side switching
options.D: Chasm crossing

2yr-13.explanation: Side switching is movement across roles within the same platform ecosystem.

2yr-13.stem: A social enterprise earns revenue and also measures social outcomes. That fits best with:

options.A: Social entrepreneurship definition used in this chapter
options.B: Decline-stage harvest strategy
options.C: Strategic entrepreneurship only
options.D: Pure imitation strategy

2yr-13.explanation: Social entrepreneurship integrates mission with viable venture logic.

2yr-13.stem: Airbnb scales supply without owning hotels mainly because it:

options.A: Vertically integrates real estate to lower costs
options.B: Unlocks external supply through hosts in an asset-light manner
options.C: Eliminates the need for governance because trust is automatic
options.D: Crosses the chasm by targeting laggards first

2yr-13.explanation: Platforms scale by enrolling ecosystem participants rather than owning assets.

2yr-13.stem: Chicken-or-egg problem at launch is best solved by:

options.A: Removing all rules to maximize entry
options.B: Waiting until both sides are naturally large
options.C: Seeding/subsidizing one side to create early transactions
options.D: Raising fees early to signal quality

2yr-13.explanation: Platforms seed one side to create proof that attracts the other side.

2yr-13.stem: Fraud/spam drives users away on a marketplace. The key platform lesson is:

options.A: Governance matters only for pipelines with inventory
options.B: Governance always hurts adoption; remove rules immediately
options.C: Governance is irrelevant; network effects are mechanical
options.D: Governance sustains trust; weak rules can collapse network effects

2yr-13.explanation: Platforms must govern participation quality; trust failures reduce participation and value.

2yr-13.stem: More merchants accept a card network → more consumers carry it → more merchants join. This is:

options.A: Decline-stage replacement demand
options.B: Cross-side network effects
options.C: Economies of scale only
options.D: Radical innovation automatically

2yr-13.explanation: Two-sided platforms benefit when each side’s participation increases value for the other.

2yr-13.stem: Multi-homing best describes:

options.A: A participant using multiple platforms at the same time
options.B: A participant switching from consumer to producer
options.C: A firm shifting from incremental to radical innovation
options.D: A firm moving from introduction to maturity stage

2yr-13.explanation: Multi-homing is simultaneous participation across platforms.

2yr-13.stem: Platform vs pipeline is best distinguished by whether the firm:

options.A: Orchestrates interactions among external parties or owns production linearly
options.B: Operates globally or locally
options.C: Uses technology or not
options.D: Is venture-funded or not

2yr-13.explanation: Core distinction: matching/orchestration vs linear production/ownership.

2yr-13.stem: Social entrepreneurship (as used here) is best described as:

options.A: Pursuing social goals via ventures using triple-bottom-line performance
options.B: Platform-only strategy because networks create all social value
options.C: Maximizing profit only and treating impact as externality
options.D: Radical-only innovation because incremental cannot help society

2yr-13.explanation: Social entrepreneurship integrates mission with venture logic and triple-bottom-line metrics.

2yr-13.stem: Strategic entrepreneurship is best described as:

options.A: Copying incumbents only to reduce novelty risk
options.B: Using strategy tools to build ventures that create and capture value
options.C: Harvesting declining markets as a startup default
options.D: Doing philanthropy first and revenue later

2yr-13.explanation: Strategic entrepreneurship applies strategic-management concepts to venture building.

2yr-13.stem: Uber’s ride-hailing model is best classified as:

options.A: Radical: new tech plus new market by definition
options.B: Pipeline: owns production and sells linearly
options.C: Incremental: cannot change industry economics
options.D: Platform: matches external producers and consumers

2yr-13.explanation: Platforms orchestrate interactions between external sides; pipelines own and push outputs.

2yr-13.stem: “Platforms always outperform pipelines.” Best caveat is:

options.A: Only if positive network effects and governance are achieved
options.B: True only with radical technology, not business design
options.C: Always true by definition, regardless of execution
options.D: True only in decline stage, not in growth stage

2yr-13.explanation: Platform outperformance depends on achieving positive network effects with governance.

2yr-13.stem: “We are a platform” but the firm owns inventory, sets prices, and sells directly. Best diagnosis:

options.A: Radical innovation because inventory implies novelty
options.B: Mostly pipeline with digital distribution
options.C: True platform because any app is multi-sided
options.D: Social entrepreneurship because intermediation helps society

2yr-13.explanation: Owning inventory and selling outputs is pipeline logic; platforms match external producers/consumers.

2yr-14.stem: A board member argues: 'Licensing is effectively ownership.' The most accurate correction is:

options.A: Licensing removes opportunism entirely, while ownership increases opportunism in practice.
options.B: Ownership is identical to licensing, since both transfer control to the buyer.
options.C: Contracts can reduce hazards, but ownership changes residual control rights and incentives.
options.D: Contracts fully replicate ownership, so governance choice is always irrelevant.

2yr-14.explanation: Ownership reallocates residual control rights and authority; contracts can never fully specify all contingencies at reasonable cost.

2yr-14.stem: A selective hybrid where Apple makes modems for some SKUs but buys for others is closest to:

options.A: A pure outsourcing choice because any external sourcing dominates governance form.
options.B: A hybrid governance arrangement that mixes make and buy to preserve benchmarking.
options.C: An unrelated diversification choice because the supplier market is separate.
options.D: A full integration choice because any internal production ends external dependence.

2yr-14.explanation: Hybrid governance sits between market and hierarchy: it can support learning and benchmarking while limiting commitment and rigidity.

2yr-14.stem: A subtle risk of internalising modems even if per-unit cost falls is:

options.A: Automatic economies of scope because modems create synergy across unrelated units.
options.B: Guaranteed legal immunity because internal ownership reduces compliance exposure.
options.C: Reduced flexibility when technology standards shift faster than internal capability can adapt.
options.D: Elimination of coordination cost because ownership removes complexity entirely.

2yr-14.explanation: Vertical integration can increase rigidity and fixed-cost commitment; the firm may be slower to pivot if standards and performance requirements change.

2yr-14.stem: Acquiring a specialist modem team (tuck-in) is best interpreted as:

options.A: A business-level positioning move that does not change firm boundaries.
options.B: A horizontal diversification into unrelated industries with no device linkage at all.
options.C: A geographic expansion into new markets because talent is distributed globally.
options.D: An instrument to move toward make by buying capability and partial control rights.

2yr-14.explanation: Tuck-ins are a mechanism of boundary change: they can accelerate internal capability and shift the firm toward 'make' without changing customer markets.

2yr-14.stem: Apple internalising a modem subsystem is vertical integration rather than horizontal diversification because:

options.A: It expands countries served, so it is geographic scope in most cases.
options.B: It changes who performs a value-chain activity, not which customer markets are served.
options.C: It changes pricing strategy, so it is business strategy by default.
options.D: It adds a new revenue stream, so it is diversification by definition.

2yr-14.explanation: Vertical integration concerns ownership/inside-outside decisions for activities in the value chain, not entry into new customer markets.

2yr-14.stem: Apple shifting from licensed Qualcomm modems to an in-house modem mainly changes which corporate strategy dimension?

options.A: Horizontal scope by entering unrelated product markets beyond device ecosystems.
options.B: Vertical scope by internalising an upstream activity previously purchased externally.
options.C: Business-level strategy by selecting cost leadership over differentiation in practice.
options.D: Geographic scope by widening the countries where devices are sold and supported.

2yr-14.explanation: Internalising a component stage moves an activity from market to firm, changing vertical boundaries (vertical integration scope). It is not a geographic or horizontal diversification move.

2yr-14.stem: Continuing to rely on Qualcomm under licensing is best classified on the make-or-buy continuum as:

options.A: A parent-subsidiary relation because licensing implies ownership and integration.
options.B: A make choice because licensing implies internal production and ownership control.
options.C: A buy choice using contracts/licensing with residual control rights staying external.
options.D: A joint venture because both parties share governance and operating decisions.

2yr-14.explanation: Licensing/purchasing is 'buy' governance: the activity remains outside firm boundaries and residual control rights stay with the supplier.

2yr-14.stem: If Apple buys an unrelated insurance business with no competence transfer, that is:

options.A: Unrelated diversification beyond a single market without synergy basis.
options.B: A geographic scope move because insurance is regulated nationally.
options.C: Backward vertical integration into upstream component production and supply.
options.D: Forward vertical integration into downstream distribution of device products.

2yr-14.explanation: This changes horizontal scope into an unrelated industry; absent competence transfer, it is unrelated diversification.

2yr-14.stem: If Apple expects rapid modem standard shifts, the most defensible first move is often:

options.A: Immediate geographic expansion because standards vary by country always.
options.B: Immediate full integration because volatility makes contracts unenforceable.
options.C: Hybrid governance that preserves flexibility while building internal capability gradually.
options.D: Immediate unrelated diversification to hedge the risk through portfolio logic.

2yr-14.explanation: Under uncertainty, hybrids can preserve flexibility and allow learning; full integration can lock the firm into fixed costs and rigid commitments.

2yr-14.stem: If Apple internalises modems mainly to weaken supplier bargaining power, the motive is closest to:

options.A: Building economies of scope by sharing capabilities across unrelated businesses.
options.B: Expanding geographic scope by entering new countries with different regulation.
options.C: Increasing market power by reducing dependence on an external bottleneck partner.
options.D: Reducing risk by diversifying across unrelated industries and financial assets.

2yr-14.explanation: A growth motive in Chapter 8 is market power: reducing dependence on a powerful supplier can increase bargaining leverage, though it may raise internal costs.

2yr-14.stem: If Apple internalises to reduce renegotiation hazard and dependence, the best theoretical justification is:

options.A: Platform logic under cross-side network effects and multi-homing behavior.
options.B: Blue-ocean logic under value innovation and new-demand creation dynamics.
options.C: Industry life-cycle logic under introduction and shakeout stage pressures.
options.D: Transaction-cost logic under contracting hazards and asset specificity concerns.

2yr-14.explanation: Chapter 8 uses transaction-cost reasoning: when markets are risky due to hazards (e.g., opportunism, enforceability), internalisation can reduce total governance cost.

2yr-14.stem: If Apple makes modems for one product line mainly to learn while buying for iPhones, the cleanest label is:

options.A: A full backward integration move that eliminates reliance on external suppliers fully.
options.B: A staged hybrid that uses internal production for learning and external sourcing for benchmarking.
options.C: A geographic scope shift because product lines are sold in different regions.
options.D: A related diversification move because product lines are different industries in effect.

2yr-14.explanation: Selective internalisation is a learning-and-benchmarking hybrid on the make-or-buy continuum; it is not full integration.

2yr-14.stem: If Apple uses long-horizon contracts plus partial internal production, the best label is:

options.A: A pure buy choice because any contract implies external governance only.
options.B: A portfolio of governance forms chosen to minimise total transaction and coordination costs.
options.C: A geographic scope choice because contracts differ across regions in practice.
options.D: A pure make choice because internal production exists at least somewhere.

2yr-14.explanation: Firms can mix governance forms by activity, product line, or region; the goal is to reduce total governance costs while preserving capability and flexibility.

2yr-14.stem: The most disciplined Chapter 8 test for the modem decision is whether:

options.A: Short-run margin rises, because corporate strategy is always a quarterly choice.
options.B: Total value created exceeds governance, coordination, and capability-build costs.
options.C: Competitor imitation occurs quickly, because imitation signals strategic correctness.
options.D: Media sentiment improves, because corporate scope is primarily reputational capital.

2yr-14.explanation: Corporate strategy is judged by net value creation: benefits (cost, quality, risk) must exceed coordination costs, rigidity, and capability-development burdens.

2yr-14.stem: Which action is least likely to be a corporate strategy move under Chapter 8 framing?

options.A: Optimising an internal modem-testing protocol without changing ownership boundaries.
options.B: Forming an equity alliance to share control rights over a key input.
options.C: Divesting a business unit to reduce horizontal scope and complexity.
options.D: Acquiring a supplier capability to internalise a value-chain stage.

2yr-14.explanation: Corporate strategy concerns scope and boundaries; internal process improvement is operational effectiveness within existing boundaries.

2yr-14.stem: Which choice is an example of a boundary alternative to full integration emphasized in Chapter 8?

options.A: Unrelated diversification into finance to hedge volatility in chip supply markets.
options.B: Long-horizon contracts or equity alliances that align incentives without full ownership.
options.C: Geographic expansion into new countries while keeping sourcing unchanged.
options.D: Spot-market bidding with frequent switching to maximize short-term flexibility.

2yr-14.explanation: Alternatives include longer contracts, equity alliances, joint ventures, and taper/hybrid approaches that reduce hazards without full ownership.

2yr-14.stem: Which governance form sits closest to 'make' on the continuum?

options.A: Equity alliance with partial ownership but shared control rights.
options.B: Full internal performance of the activity within the firm's boundary.
options.C: Long-term contracting with penalties and audit clauses for performance.
options.D: Spot purchasing from multiple suppliers with rapid switching ability.

2yr-14.explanation: Full internal performance is closest to 'make' because residual control rights are inside the firm; the others remain external or hybrid.

2yr-14.stem: Which is NOT one of Chapter 8's three corporate strategy dimensions?

options.A: Geographic scope across regions and national markets.
options.B: Innovation cadence and imitation timing across technology life cycles.
options.C: Vertical integration scope along the value chain stages.
options.D: Horizontal diversification scope beyond one product-market domain.

2yr-14.explanation: Chapter 8 assesses corporate strategy along vertical scope, horizontal scope, and geographic scope. Innovation cadence is treated elsewhere in the text.

2yr-14.stem: Which is the best 'non-intuitive' warning when executives say 'control is always good'?

options.A: Control always improves margins because internal costs are always lower.
options.B: Control can be value destroying when added coordination and rigidity exceed benefits.
options.C: Control always reduces scrutiny because regulators prefer integrated firms.
options.D: Control always eliminates risk because ownership removes uncertainty completely.

2yr-14.explanation: Chapter 8 stresses that corporate moves must create net value; control can increase cost, reduce flexibility, and raise liability.

2yr-14.stem: Which is the most accurate description of 'vertical market failure' in Chapter 8?

options.A: Markets are global so vertical integration is legally impossible everywhere in practice at scale.
options.B: Markets create scope economies automatically so diversification is unnecessary in practice at scale.
options.C: Markets along the value chain are too risky and alternatives too costly in time or money.
options.D: Markets are perfectly competitive so the firm should always buy the activity in practice.

2yr-14.explanation: Vertical market failure occurs when market governance is too risky or alternatives too costly, making integration or hybrids attractive.

2yr-14.stem: Which of the following best fits a diversification premium condition?

options.A: Unrelated businesses reduce risk, so valuations always rise above sum-of-parts.
options.B: Shared capabilities create economies of scope that exceed added coordination costs.
options.C: Geographic expansion always creates synergy, so valuations rise mechanically.
options.D: Spinouts always destroy value because internal markets are weakened.

2yr-14.explanation: A premium requires real scope economies or other value creation exceeding the costs of complexity; unrelated risk reduction alone is not guaranteed to create premiums.

2yr-14.stem: Which option is most likely to increase legal exposure rather than reduce it?

options.A: Keeping activity external under licensing with supplier bearing some obligations.
options.B: Using a joint venture where liabilities are ring-fenced by governance terms.
options.C: Using long-horizon contracts with explicit audit rights and service levels.
options.D: Owning and operating sensitive design and compliance processes inside the firm.

2yr-14.explanation: Internalisation can increase compliance responsibilities and legal exposure; outsourcing or structured governance can sometimes shift or share that burden.

2yr-14.stem: Which statement best captures why 'make' can raise cost even when the supplier is expensive?

options.A: Internal units guarantee scale economies bigger than the whole industry.
options.B: Internal units eliminate fixed costs because capex disappears in practice.
options.C: Internal units can lose market discipline and create higher overhead over time.
options.D: Internal units always face more competition, which forces costs down sharply.

2yr-14.explanation: Chapter 8 notes in-house suppliers may not be exposed to competitive pressure, potentially increasing cost structures and inefficiency.

2yr-14.stem: Which statement best describes why 'shorter option is correct' is unreliable here?

options.A: Option length is controlled, so correctness depends on concept logic not style.
options.B: Option length signals expertise, so longer options are always correct.
options.C: Option length is irrelevant because all corporate strategy is subjective.
options.D: Option length signals difficulty, so shorter options are always correct.

2yr-14.explanation: The quiz is designed so option length does not cue correctness; students must apply the Chapter 8 logic precisely.

2yr-14.stem: Which statement most precisely separates corporate strategy from business strategy in this case?

options.A: Corporate strategy sets marketing spend; business strategy sets diversification typology only.
options.B: Corporate strategy sets pricing tactics; business strategy sets ownership boundaries and scope.
options.C: Corporate strategy sets HR policy; business strategy sets geography and vertical scope.
options.D: Corporate strategy sets firm boundaries; business strategy sets how to compete within an arena.

2yr-14.explanation: Chapter 8 treats corporate strategy as boundary and scope decisions (vertical/horizontal/geographic). Business strategy concerns competitive positioning within a given industry.

2yr-14.stem: A delivery joint venture is best classified as:

options.A: A geographic expansion arrangement because partners operate in multiple states.
options.B: A hybrid governance arrangement with shared control rights and joint decision making.
options.C: A parent-subsidiary arrangement with full control and no shared governance rights.
options.D: A spot-market arrangement where switching is costless and continuity is absent.

2yr-14.explanation: Joint ventures create shared governance and allocate control rights; they are intermediate forms on the make-or-buy continuum.

2yr-14.stem: A delivery joint venture is best classified as:

options.A: A spot-market arrangement where switching is costless and continuity is absent.
options.B: A parent-subsidiary arrangement with full control and no shared governance rights.
options.C: A hybrid governance arrangement with shared control rights and joint decision making.
options.D: A geographic expansion arrangement because partners operate in multiple states.

2yr-14.explanation: Joint ventures create shared governance and allocate control rights; they are intermediate forms on the make-or-buy continuum.

2yr-14.stem: A non-intuitive risk of full forward integration into last-mile delivery is:

options.A: Elimination of legal and safety compliance because internal fleets reduce scrutiny.
options.B: Higher fixed cost and reduced flexibility when demand or labor conditions shift.
options.C: Guaranteed on-time performance because internal delivery always outperforms in practice.
options.D: Automatic reduction of coordination burdens because ownership removes conflict.

2yr-14.explanation: Chapter 8 warns integration can reduce flexibility and raise fixed costs; regulatory and labor constraints may increase internal complexity.

2yr-14.stem: Amazon expanding delivery stations and rural coverage is best classified as:

options.A: Unrelated diversification into transport manufacturing with no e-commerce linkage.
options.B: Backward vertical integration into upstream packaging materials and supplier stages.
options.C: Geographic scope expansion only because facilities are domestic and regional.
options.D: Forward vertical integration into downstream fulfilment and last-mile delivery capacity.

2yr-14.explanation: Owning more distribution nodes and delivery capacity internalises downstream activities, which is forward vertical integration in the value chain.

2yr-14.stem: Claim: 'This is only geography, not corporate strategy.' Best correction is:

options.A: Facilities can still change vertical scope by internalising activities previously outsourced.
options.B: It is unrelated diversification because delivery is a different industry.
options.C: Only mergers change boundaries, so facility build-out is operational only.
options.D: Domestic facilities never change boundaries because they remain in one country.

2yr-14.explanation: A corporate boundary shift can occur within a country; internalisation changes who performs the activity.

2yr-14.stem: If Amazon internalises last-mile mainly to reduce carrier bargaining power, the motive is:

options.A: Risk reduction by unrelated diversification across non-logistics business units.
options.B: Geographic scope expansion because bargaining differs by country regulation.
options.C: Market power by reducing dependence on a bottleneck partner and improving leverage.
options.D: Economies of scope because carriers create synergy across unrelated industries.

2yr-14.explanation: Reducing dependence on a powerful partner can increase leverage; it is a market power motive, not diversification.

2yr-14.stem: If Amazon uses USPS for low-density routes but its own fleet for dense routes, this is:

options.A: An unrelated diversification strategy because route types are different industries.
options.B: A full buy strategy because any USPS use implies markets dominate governance.
options.C: A full make strategy because any internal delivery ends all outsourcing.
options.D: A selective hybrid boundary strategy balancing cost economics of density.

2yr-14.explanation: This is selective internalisation: governance differs by route economics; it is a hybrid strategy.

2yr-14.stem: If delivery quality is observable but contract enforcement is costly, the best implication is:

options.A: Integration never helps because contracts can fully specify and enforce quality.
options.B: Governance may shift toward hybrids or internalisation to secure performance.
options.C: Geographic expansion solves enforcement by averaging quality across regions.
options.D: Markets perfectly replicate ownership because observability solves enforcement.

2yr-14.explanation: Even observable performance can be hard to enforce due to monitoring and legal costs; governance may change accordingly.

2yr-14.stem: In Chapter 8 terms, building new delivery stations primarily changes:

options.A: Vertical scope by internalising distribution capacity and fulfilment activities.
options.B: Geographic scope by entering new countries and new regulatory jurisdictions.
options.C: Business strategy by repositioning in rivalry without boundary changes.
options.D: Horizontal scope by entering unrelated markets with no competence overlap.

2yr-14.explanation: This is a boundary/vertical scope decision (distribution stage ownership), not horizontal diversification.

2yr-14.stem: In Chapter 8 terms, building new delivery stations primarily changes:

options.A: Horizontal scope by entering unrelated markets with no competence overlap.
options.B: Business strategy by repositioning in rivalry without boundary changes.
options.C: Geographic scope by entering new countries and new regulatory jurisdictions.
options.D: Vertical scope by internalising distribution capacity and fulfilment activities.

2yr-14.explanation: This is a boundary/vertical scope decision (distribution stage ownership), not horizontal diversification.

2yr-14.stem: In Chapter 8 terms, building new delivery stations primarily changes:

options.A: Geographic scope by entering new countries and new regulatory jurisdictions.
options.B: Vertical scope by internalising distribution capacity and fulfilment activities.
options.C: Horizontal scope by entering unrelated markets with no competence overlap.
options.D: Business strategy by repositioning in rivalry without boundary changes.

2yr-15.stem: A non-intuitive failure mode if Amazon moves from BORROW to BUY too quickly is:

options.A: Integration overload: coordination costs rise faster than synergies materialise.
options.B: Legal insulation: ownership reduces compliance exposure relative to partnerships.
options.C: Learning acceleration: acquisitions always increase learning speed over time.
options.D: Guaranteed economies: acquisitions always lower total cost at scale.

2yr-15.explanation: Rapid acquisitions can create integration overload—coordination, culture, systems—and destroy value before synergies appear.

2yr-15.stem: A subtle reason Amazon may prefer BORROW over BUY for frontier AI capability is:

options.A: Regulatory immunity: acquisitions reduce scrutiny more than alliances.
options.B: Agency benefit: acquisitions always reduce internal coordination costs.
options.C: Option value: staged commitment preserves flexibility under rapid technical change.
options.D: Guaranteed synergy: acquisitions always outperform contracts in dynamic markets.

2yr-15.explanation: Borrowing via equity alliances can preserve option value and flexibility, while acquisitions create rigidity and integration burdens.

2yr-15.stem: A subtle signal that Amazon is pursuing ‘option value’ in this deal is most consistent with:

options.A: Divestiture of the capability provider to reduce exposure and uncertainty.
options.B: Minority stake with staged investments rather than an immediate full acquisition.
options.C: Immediate cash tender offer that transfers 100% control on day one.
options.D: Merger of equals with joint headquarters and one unified brand instantly.

2yr-15.explanation: Staged investments and minority positions preserve flexibility and resemble real options; they are not the same as full integration.

2yr-15.stem: Amazon’s minority stake plus deep technical collaboration with Anthropic is best classified as which growth pathway?

options.A: Build: internal development because minority equity equals internal capability.
options.B: Exit: divest because resource gaps are better solved by retrenchment.
options.C: Buy: acquisition because a minority stake implies majority control in practice.
options.D: Borrow: access to resources via alliance governance without full ownership integration.

2yr-15.explanation: Minority equity plus collaboration is a BORROW pathway (equity alliance), not an acquisition (BUY) and not pure internal development (BUILD).

2yr-15.stem: If Amazon fears that a non‑equity alliance will suffer from weak ties and limited trust, Chapter 9 suggests moving toward:

options.A: Pure spot-market sourcing because weaker ties increase trust in most cases.
options.B: Pure internal development because all alliances fail under uncertainty.
options.C: Immediate acquisition because any trust concern implies buy is always best.
options.D: Equity alliance governance to strengthen ties and increase commitment signals.

2yr-15.explanation: Equity alliances can strengthen ties and commitment relative to purely contractual alliances, while still avoiding full integration.

2yr-15.stem: If Amazon finds the partner resource is highly tradable but requires only low closeness, the most defensible ‘borrow’ form is usually:

options.A: A full internal build because tradability makes markets unreliable.
options.B: A contract-based non‑equity alliance such as licensing or service access terms.
options.C: A joint venture because low closeness implies shared entity governance.
options.D: An acquisition because tradability implies ownership transfer is required.

2yr-15.explanation: High tradability with low closeness points to borrowing via contract (non‑equity). JVs or acquisitions imply deeper commitment than needed.

2yr-15.stem: If Amazon’s goal is to learn a new capability (frontier-model development), the most appropriate governance concern is to design mechanisms for:

options.A: Knowledge sharing while protecting against opportunism and leakage risks.
options.B: Industry entry deterrence through predatory pricing and capacity preemption.
options.C: Immediate full consolidation because learning requires ownership by default.
options.D: Pure price-based contracting because learning is fully tradable as a commodity.

2yr-15.explanation: Learning alliances require knowledge-sharing routines and governance to reduce opportunism and leakage—key themes in Chapter 9 alliance effectiveness.

2yr-15.stem: If Amazon’s internal resources are not relevant and the target capability is not tradable, but closeness need is LOW, the framework next asks mainly:

options.A: Whether the deal would increase the bargaining power of suppliers materially.
options.B: Whether a non-equity contract can be written with complete contingency coverage.
options.C: Whether integration capability is high enough to justify an acquisition pathway.
options.D: Whether the alliance will reduce rivalry by horizontal integration alone.

2yr-15.explanation: With low tradability and low need for closeness, the framework turns to integration feasibility: if high, BUY; if low, revisit pathways.

2yr-15.stem: If a capability is not easily tradable and Amazon needs high closeness with a partner to access it, the framework pushes toward:

options.A: Divest the initiative because the resource gap cannot be closed in practice.
options.B: Build internally because closeness makes alliances infeasible in practice at scale.
options.C: Borrow via a deeper alliance form such as equity alliance or joint venture.
options.D: Buy immediately because closeness always implies acquisition necessity in practice at scale.

2yr-15.explanation: When tradability is low and closeness is high, the framework escalates to deeper BORROW forms (equity/JV) before BUY.

2yr-15.stem: If the alliance is meant to enter new markets with lower upfront commitment, the closest ‘why enter alliances’ reason is:

options.A: Market entry with risk sharing rather than full ownership commitment.
options.B: Corporate diversification into unrelated industries to reduce volatility.
options.C: Vertical integration to internalise upstream suppliers for cost advantage.
options.D: Horizontal integration to eliminate competitors and reduce rivalry quickly.

2yr-15.explanation: Alliances commonly support market entry and risk sharing; vertical/horizontal integration are ownership-based corporate moves.

2yr-15.stem: In Chapter 9 terms, the most precise way to distinguish BORROW via contract from BORROW via equity/JV is:

options.A: Whether the partner operates in a foreign country and faces FX risk exposure.
options.B: Whether the industry is at maturity or shakeout stage in the life cycle.
options.C: Whether the firm competes via differentiation or cost leadership in practice.
options.D: Depth of commitment and closeness enabled by residual control rights allocation.

2yr-15.explanation: Equity/JV governance allocates stronger residual rights and commitment than pure contracts, enabling greater closeness but reducing flexibility.

2yr-15.stem: In Chapter 9, an alliance is ‘strategic’ only if it can plausibly:

options.A: Remove all uncertainty by guaranteeing outcomes through complete contracts in practice.
options.B: Affect competitive advantage by increasing value and/or lowering costs meaningfully in practice.
options.C: Increase market share in the short run even if unit economics worsen materially.
options.D: Create publicity benefits even if no capabilities or resources are exchanged.

2yr-15.explanation: Strategic alliances must have the potential to affect competitive advantage (value ↑ and/or cost ↓), not just publicity or temporary share gains.

2yr-15.stem: In the Chapter 9 decision sequence, if internal resources are highly relevant to closing the AI-model gap, the first recommendation is:

options.A: Build internally before considering borrow or buy pathways further.
options.B: Buy the target because integration is easier than internal learning.
options.C: Form a JV because closeness is always required for advanced AI.
options.D: Borrow via a contract because tradability always dominates relevancy.

2yr-15.explanation: If internal resources are relevant (similar and superior/VRIO‑like), BUILD is recommended before external pathways.

2yr-15.stem: In ‘how to make alliances work’ logic, the combination that most directly strengthens effective alliance governance is:

options.A: Economies of scale, experience curves, and learning curves in production.
options.B: Bargaining power, switching costs, and rivalry intensity in the five forces.
options.C: Differentiation drivers, complements, and blue‑ocean value innovation in practice.
options.D: Relation‑specific investments, knowledge‑sharing routines, and interfirm trust in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: Chapter 9 emphasises three reinforcing elements for effective alliance governance: relation-specific investments, knowledge-sharing routines, and trust.

2yr-15.stem: Only after low relevancy, low tradability, and a high need for closeness, the final gate to consider BUY is primarily:

options.A: Whether the acquirer’s stock price rises the week the deal is announced.
options.B: Whether the alliance has weak ties and therefore must always be abandoned.
options.C: Whether post‑deal integration capability is high enough to capture value.
options.D: Whether the target has a famous founder and strong media narratives.

2yr-15.explanation: BUY requires an additional integration feasibility check; weak integration capability is a classic M&A value-destruction channel.

2yr-15.stem: Suppose Amazon’s internal model assets are NOT relevant, but frontier capability is highly tradable through contracts. The framework points first to:

options.A: Borrow through contract governance rather than acquiring the capability provider.
options.B: Buy through acquisition because contracts are too weak to govern resources.
options.C: Build internally because tradability is irrelevant when relevancy is low.
options.D: Delay the decision because integration must be tested before borrowing.

2yr-15.explanation: Low relevancy + high tradability implies BORROW through contracts/licensing rather than immediate acquisition.

2yr-15.stem: The most non‑intuitive risk of equity alliances versus non‑equity alliances is:

options.A: Higher speed of entry/exit because equity is easier than contracts.
options.B: No governance risk because ownership automatically resolves all conflicts.
options.C: Lower need for trust because minority ownership substitutes for routines.
options.D: Reduced flexibility if the partner pivots strategy, because exit is costlier.

2yr-15.explanation: Equity alliances can reduce flexibility and make exit harder; they do not substitute fully for trust or governance routines.

2yr-15.stem: When moving from alliance formation to post‑formation management, the most diagnostic metric is:

options.A: Whether executive compensation rises relative to peer group immediately.
options.B: Whether press mentions increase quarter-over-quarter after announcement in practice.
options.C: Whether competitor stock prices fall in the week following disclosure.
options.D: Whether joint routines and trust are improving resource combination performance.

2yr-15.explanation: Alliance value comes from how well the partners combine resources over time; routines and trust are leading indicators versus publicity measures.

2yr-15.stem: Which governance form most strongly increases commitment yet risks ‘two bosses’ and slower negotiation?

options.A: Equity alliance with small stake and minimal operational coordination.
options.B: Joint venture with shared governance, potentially creating dual reporting lines.
options.C: Simple supplier contract with spot-market pricing and rapid switching.
options.D: Non‑equity alliance with short contract and easy termination rights.

2yr-15.explanation: Joint ventures tend to create the strongest ties and commitment but can cause complex governance, slow setup, and dual reporting issues.

2yr-15.stem: Which governance form usually offers the highest flexibility and fastest entry/exit?

options.A: Joint venture governed by a jointly owned entity and shared reporting lines.
options.B: Non‑equity alliance governed mainly by contract terms and performance clauses.
options.C: Equity alliance governed by minority ownership and cross-investment rights in practice.
options.D: Acquisition governed by full ownership and hierarchical integration in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: Non‑equity alliances are typically most flexible and quick; deeper governance forms increase commitment but reduce flexibility.

2yr-15.stem: Which is the best reason Amazon might avoid BUY even if integration looks feasible?

options.A: Regulatory scrutiny and concentration risk can destroy the expected net value.
options.B: Acquisitions always raise value because they remove contracting costs completely.
options.C: Buy is always faster than borrow because ownership removes negotiations.
options.D: Buy always reduces cultural integration risk because systems are unified.

2yr-15.explanation: Even feasible integration can be undermined by regulatory scrutiny and concentration risks; M&A is not automatically faster or lower-risk.

2yr-15.stem: Which motive best fits Amazon’s alliance with Anthropic if the goal is to hedge uncertainty in generative AI trajectory?

options.A: Improve vertical scope through backward integration into chip manufacturing.
options.B: Reduce rivalry via horizontal integration in a consolidated market structure.
options.C: Hedge against uncertainty while accessing complementary resources externally.
options.D: Lock in distribution by acquiring downstream retail channels.

2yr-15.explanation: Alliances are often used to hedge uncertainty and access complementary resources without committing to full acquisition.

2yr-15.stem: Which statement best captures why BORROW can be superior to BUILD for Amazon in frontier AI?

options.A: Borrow prevents leakage automatically because partners cannot learn anything in practice.
options.B: Borrow can close a capability gap faster than internal development in time‑critical races.
options.C: Borrow eliminates uncertainty because contracts specify all future contingencies in practice.
options.D: Borrow is always cheaper because partners bear all costs without compensation.
