2yr-15.explanation: Borrowing can be faster than building in fast-moving environments; it does not eliminate uncertainty or leakage by itself.

2yr-15.stem: Which statement best explains why BUILD can still dominate BORROW in some cases?

options.A: If external resources are tradable, building is unnecessary and always inferior.
options.B: If integration is low, building is always slower than buying in practice.
options.C: If internal resources are relevant and superior, building can avoid leakage and dependence.
options.D: If closeness is high, building becomes impossible due to partner dependence.

2yr-15.explanation: Relevant and superior internal resources can make BUILD best, avoiding dependence and knowledge leakage associated with external partnerships.

2yr-15.stem: A non-intuitive advantage of non‑equity alliances is that they can:

options.A: Make culture integration easier because no people or systems are involved.
options.B: Guarantee appropriation of partner know-how because data is transferred fully.
options.C: Enable rapid experimentation across partners without absorbing full integration costs.
options.D: Eliminate opportunism risk because contracts fully specify all contingencies.

2yr-15.explanation: Non‑equity alliances can support experimentation and speed; they do not eliminate opportunism, and they still require coordination despite not integrating organisations.

2yr-15.stem: A non‑intuitive reason Apple might avoid equity alliance governance in this case is:

options.A: Equity automatically removes reputational risk because ownership signals control.
options.B: Equity eliminates all contracting costs and therefore dominates in dynamic markets.
options.C: Equity guarantees better privacy because minority stakes enforce compliance.
options.D: Equity reduces exit flexibility if model performance or policy constraints shift.

2yr-15.explanation: Equity alliances can lock firms into partners and reduce flexibility—costly under fast change. They do not guarantee privacy or reputational safety.

2yr-15.stem: A robust way to reduce opportunism in knowledge-sharing alliances is to increase:

options.A: Relation-specific investments that raise the cost of defection for both sides.
options.B: One-sided dependence so the stronger party can threaten exit immediately.
options.C: Secrecy so no knowledge routines exist and collaboration stays superficial.
options.D: Spot-market switching frequency so partners have no incentive to commit.

2yr-15.explanation: Relation-specific investments increase mutual commitment; combined with routines and trust, they support effective alliance governance.

2yr-15.stem: An alliance is ‘strategic’ for Apple only if it can plausibly:

options.A: Eliminate rival entry by instantly creating monopolistic market power in practice.
options.B: Increase value and/or lower costs in a way that affects competitive advantage.
options.C: Increase press coverage and developer excitement without capability exchange in practice.
options.D: Reduce uncertainty to zero by fully contracting all future contingencies.

2yr-15.explanation: A strategic alliance must have the potential to affect competitive advantage (value/cost), not just publicity or impossible complete contracting.

2yr-15.stem: Apple integrating ChatGPT without an ownership stake is best classified as which alliance governance mechanism?

options.A: Acquisition governed by full ownership and hierarchical integration in practice.
options.B: Joint venture governed by a new jointly owned entity with shared management.
options.C: Non‑equity alliance governed primarily by contractual access and technical integration.
options.D: Equity alliance governed by minority ownership and board-level control rights.

2yr-15.explanation: The Apple–OpenAI integration is a non‑equity partnership (contractual/technical integration), not an equity alliance, JV, or acquisition.

2yr-15.stem: Effective alliance governance is most likely to fail first when Apple and OpenAI do NOT:

options.A: Assume that trust will emerge automatically without deliberate mechanisms in practice.
options.B: Define knowledge boundaries and escalation paths for conflict resolution in practice.
options.C: Invest in relation-specific assets and routines that make collaboration productive.
options.D: Choose a governance form with a clearly defined scope and decision rights.

2yr-15.explanation: Without relation-specific investments and routines, alliances remain superficial and fail to create valuable resource combinations; trust does not arise automatically.

2yr-15.stem: For Apple, the MOST Chapter‑9‑consistent reason to prefer a non‑equity alliance here is:

options.A: Guaranteed appropriation because contracts eliminate knowledge leakage entirely.
options.B: High flexibility with lower commitment while accessing complementary capability quickly.
options.C: Guaranteed internal learning speed because partners are fully integrated.
options.D: Guaranteed antitrust immunity because alliances are never scrutinised by regulators.

2yr-15.explanation: Non‑equity alliances are flexible and fast; they do not eliminate leakage or regulatory scrutiny, and they are not equivalent to integration.

2yr-15.stem: If Apple expands the partnership into a jointly owned AI-services entity, the governance shifts primarily to:

options.A: Non‑equity alliance governance with short duration and easy exit rights.
options.B: Joint venture governance with strongest tie and highest coordination demands.
options.C: Acquisition governance with immediate unilateral control by one firm.
options.D: Equity alliance governance with minimal coordination and maximum flexibility.

2yr-15.explanation: A jointly owned operating entity is a JV; it typically increases commitment, coordination, and governance complexity.

2yr-15.stem: If Apple later bought a minority stake in OpenAI to gain a window into technology and commitment, the governance mechanism shifts toward:

options.A: Non‑equity alliance governance with weaker ties than before in practice.
options.B: Acquisition governance implying immediate majority control and integration.
options.C: Equity alliance governance with stronger ties than pure contractual collaboration.
options.D: Joint venture governance requiring a new jointly owned operating entity.

2yr-15.explanation: Minority ownership is an equity alliance: stronger ties and option value, but less flexibility than non‑equity contracting.

2yr-15.stem: If Apple uses the alliance mainly to learn, the most appropriate post‑formation capability is:

options.A: Alliance management capability: dedicated processes to manage learning and conflict.
options.B: Porter positioning capability: choose cost leadership to prevent knowledge leakage.
options.C: Vertical integration capability: build upstream suppliers to avoid learning needs.
options.D: Diversification capability: add unrelated businesses to stabilise learning budgets.

2yr-15.explanation: Alliance management capability (partnering skills, governance routines, conflict resolution) improves alliance performance and learning outcomes.

2yr-15.stem: If Apple’s key risk is knowledge leakage while learning from OpenAI, the most relevant governance design response is to strengthen:

options.A: Five-forces positioning because governance does not affect learning outcomes.
options.B: Price-based switching ability by shortening contracts to weekly renewals.
options.C: Knowledge-sharing routines with safeguards and boundaries for information flows.
options.D: Pure acquisition logic because leakage is solved only by ownership.

2yr-15.explanation: Alliance effectiveness depends on knowledge-sharing routines and trust; governance should define what is shared, how, and with what protections.

2yr-15.stem: If Apple’s priority is privacy perception, the best Chapter‑9 governance inference is:

options.A: Acquisition is required because privacy cannot be contractually enforced in practice.
options.B: Non‑equity alliance can be viable if decision rights and data boundaries are explicit.
options.C: Joint venture is required because privacy requires a new jointly owned entity.
options.D: Equity alliance is required because privacy can be governed only by ownership.

2yr-15.explanation: Privacy can be governed through contractual decision rights, auditing, and boundaries; ownership is not the only mechanism, though enforcement costs matter.

2yr-15.stem: If an alliance increases value but also increases cost, it remains strategic only if:

options.A: The alliance is public, because publicity is a proxy for strategic impact.
options.B: Net value improves relative to alternatives, affecting competitive advantage materially.
options.C: The contract is long, because duration alone defines strategic importance.
options.D: The partner is famous, because brand association creates value automatically.

2yr-15.explanation: Strategic importance requires net value creation relative to alternatives, not merely duration, publicity, or brand association.

2yr-15.stem: In the ‘how alliances work’ logic, interfirm trust most directly enables:

options.A: Higher rivalry intensity and stronger threat of entry across the industry.
options.B: Higher buyer switching costs through proprietary product complements in practice.
options.C: Lower monitoring costs and faster knowledge exchange without constant verification.
options.D: A steeper experience curve and lower unit costs in internal manufacturing.

2yr-15.explanation: Trust reduces monitoring and facilitates knowledge exchange, supporting effective governance and resource combination performance.

2yr-15.stem: Suppose Apple wants to internalise the capability rather than borrow it. Under build‑borrow‑buy, the key gate that justifies BUILD is:

options.A: High relevancy of internal resources to solve the resource gap and outperform rivals.
options.B: High integration ability because integration is the same as internal development.
options.C: High tradability of targeted resources because contracts guarantee transfer always in practice.
options.D: High closeness need because closeness makes building superior by default in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: BUILD is favoured when internal resources are relevant (similar, superior/VRIO-like), making internal development effective and less dependent on partners.

2yr-15.stem: The most diagnostic signal that Apple should consider BUY rather than BORROW is:

options.A: High tradability plus low closeness need, combined with weak integration capability.
options.B: Low relevancy plus high tradability, combined with no need for closeness.
options.C: Low tradability plus high closeness need, combined with strong integration capability.
options.D: High relevancy of internal resources, combined with high tradability externally.

2yr-15.explanation: BUY becomes plausible only after earlier gates: low relevancy, low tradability, high closeness need, then integration feasibility; otherwise borrow/build dominates.

2yr-15.stem: The most precise disadvantage of a purely contractual alliance for Apple is:

options.A: Guaranteed regulatory rejection because contracts trigger antitrust bans in practice at scale.
options.B: Weaker ties can reduce trust and commitment relative to equity or JV forms.
options.C: Guaranteed inability to learn because contracts prevent any knowledge sharing in practice.
options.D: Higher fixed costs and integration risk relative to acquiring the partner fully.

2yr-15.explanation: Contracts can create weaker ties, limiting trust and commitment. They do not necessarily imply high integration risk or automatic regulatory rejection.

2yr-15.stem: The most precise downside of a JV compared with an equity alliance is:

options.A: Lower commitment and weaker ties relative to non‑equity contract governance.
options.B: Higher negotiation cost and governance complexity with potentially dual reporting lines.
options.C: No need for trust because a JV guarantees alignment through contracts.
options.D: Higher exit flexibility because a JV can be dissolved instantly without cost.

2yr-15.explanation: JVs tend to be costly and complex to negotiate and manage; they can create dual-reporting issues and do not eliminate trust requirements.

2yr-15.stem: Which combination best matches the Chapter‑9 reasons that firms enter alliances?

options.A: Strengthen position, enter markets, hedge uncertainty, access complements, learn capabilities.
options.B: Lower taxes, raise debt, reduce wages, increase turnover, and cut dividends.
options.C: Increase rivalry, raise entry threats, widen substitutes, and weaken buyer power.
options.D: Reduce VRIO fit, lower value, increase cost, and weaken differentiation drivers.

2yr-15.explanation: Chapter 9 lists common alliance motives: strengthen position, enter markets, hedge uncertainty, access complements, and learn capabilities.

2yr-15.stem: Which governance form would most likely be chosen if Apple needed the strongest tie and the institutional setting required shared local operation?

options.A: Non‑equity alliance that avoids shared operating decisions and new entity.
options.B: Joint venture with shared entity and stronger commitment than contracts alone.
options.C: Equity alliance with small stake and minimal coordination requirements.
options.D: Simple supplier contract with no relational governance and rapid termination.

2yr-15.explanation: JVs are the strongest alliance form and can be required by institutions; they are slower and more complex but create deeper ties.

2yr-15.stem: Which option would be a category mistake when analysing Apple–OpenAI under Chapter 9?

options.A: Treating it as alliance governance rather than a business-strategy positioning move alone.
options.B: Treating it as non‑equity borrow rather than as an outright acquisition pathway.
options.C: Treating it as a strategic alliance only if it affects value/cost advantages.
options.D: Treating it as horizontal integration that eliminates a rival competitor.

2yr-15.explanation: Apple–OpenAI is not horizontal integration; it is collaboration (borrow). Horizontal integration requires acquisition/merger among competitors.

2yr-15.stem: Which statement best characterises ‘borrow’ in build‑borrow‑buy?

options.A: Divestiture to shrink scope and abandon a strategic initiative entirely.
options.B: Majority-control acquisition followed by rapid integration of systems and people.
options.C: Access resources externally via contract, equity alliance, or JV without full acquisition.
options.D: Internal development of resources without partner involvement and without contracts.

2yr-15.explanation: Borrow refers to accessing resources via alliances/contractual arrangements rather than internal development or full acquisition.

2yr-15.stem: Which statement is the hardest trap in alliance governance for Apple?

options.A: Assuming joint ventures are always faster to form than non-equity partnerships.
options.B: Assuming alliances never affect competitive advantage and are always tactical.
options.C: Assuming equity ownership is always inferior to a short contractual arrangement.
options.D: Assuming contract terms alone substitute for interfirm trust and routines fully.

2yr-15.explanation: Contracts cannot specify everything; trust and routines matter. Overreliance on legal terms alone is a classic governance trap.

2yr-15.stem: Which ‘why enter alliances’ rationale best matches Apple seeking rapid capability complementarity without buying the capability provider?

options.A: Backward vertical integration to internalise upstream AI chip manufacturing.
options.B: Access critical complementary resources while sharing risk and preserving flexibility.
options.C: Horizontal integration to reduce rivalry by acquiring the partner fully.
options.D: Unrelated diversification to reduce risk through cash flow smoothing.

2yr-15.explanation: Alliances often access complementary resources faster and with less commitment than acquisitions, especially under uncertainty.

2yr-15.stem: Within Apple–OpenAI, the clearest ‘weak‑tie’ symptom of a non‑equity alliance would be:

options.A: Low mutual commitment that limits joint learning and slows problem resolution over time.
options.B: High integration cost because the firms must unify HR and finance systems quickly.
options.C: Guaranteed antitrust intervention because non‑equity contracts are illegal generally in practice.
options.D: Instant elimination of opportunism because contracts specify all contingencies in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: Non‑equity alliances can suffer from weak ties: lower commitment and limited trust/routines, reducing learning and joint problem solving.

2yr-15.stem: A classic JV disadvantage likely to appear in this case is:

options.A: Governance complexity where managers face dual reporting lines and slow decisions.
options.B: Guaranteed weak ties that prevent any serious knowledge sharing.
options.C: Complete inability to learn because shared entities prevent routines.
options.D: Immediate antitrust illegality because all JVs are presumptively unlawful.

2yr-15.explanation: JVs can create complex governance structures and dual reporting, slowing decisions and raising transaction/coordination costs.

2yr-15.stem: A firm has an alliance management capability advantage if it can:

options.A: Always avoid alliances because alliances cannot create competitive advantage in practice.
options.B: Always rely on short contracts because flexibility dominates commitment in practice.
options.C: Repeatedly design and manage alliances better than rivals through routines and learning.
options.D: Always choose acquisition over alliances regardless of integration feasibility in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: Alliance management capability can be a source of competitive advantage through learning-by-doing and dedicated alliance functions.

2yr-15.stem: A hard-to-guess sign the JV is failing strategically is:

options.A: Executives express strong optimism and cite long-term vision repeatedly in practice.
options.B: Press coverage remains high and positive even when delivery milestones slip.
options.C: Resource combination fails to increase value or lower cost relative to alternatives.
options.D: Stock price rises after announcement but operational synergies remain unclear.

2yr-15.explanation: Strategic success requires resource combination that improves value/cost; publicity or initial stock movements are weak indicators without operational performance.

2yr-15.stem: A key reason firms choose JVs instead of equity alliances is that JVs can:

options.A: Eliminate opportunism because joint ownership removes incentives in practice.
options.B: Maximise exit flexibility compared with non-equity contracts in practice.
options.C: Avoid the need for governance because an entity guarantees alignment.
options.D: Create an operating entity to coordinate complex joint production and learning.

2yr-15.explanation: JVs provide a vehicle to coordinate complex joint activities; they do not eliminate governance or opportunism risk automatically.

2yr-15.stem: A non-intuitive JV failure mode is:

options.A: Partners never face conflict because shared ownership forces harmony in practice.
options.B: Partners overinvest because governance makes free riding impossible in practice.
options.C: Partners underinvest because each expects the other to carry the cost burden.
options.D: Partners always innovate faster because JVs guarantee learning speed in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: JVs can suffer from underinvestment/free-riding incentives, especially if governance and accountability mechanisms are weak.

2yr-15.stem: A ‘dedicated alliance function’ strengthens VW’s alliance management capability mainly by:

options.A: Guaranteeing synergy by forcing all partners into immediate acquisition.
options.B: Capturing lessons learned and standardising governance routines across repeated partnerships.
options.C: Replacing partner selection with procurement auctions to maximise switching speed.
options.D: Eliminating the need for trust by enforcing compliance through litigation only.

2yr-15.explanation: Alliance functions institutionalise learning-by-doing, codifying best practices in partner selection, governance design, and post‑formation management.

2yr-15.stem: If Rivian fears that VW will appropriate know-how, the governance response most consistent with Chapter 9 is to:

options.A: Rely only on secrecy because any knowledge exchange destroys the alliance.
options.B: Eliminate routines so that learning cannot occur and opportunism is impossible.
options.C: Specify IP boundaries, create joint routines, and increase mutual dependence through investments.
options.D: Terminate the JV immediately because opportunism is unavoidable in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: Chapter 9 suggests combining governance safeguards with routines and relation-specific investments to reduce opportunism while enabling value creation.

2yr-15.stem: If VW wanted immediate unilateral control of the software stack, the mechanism would shift from JV to:

options.A: Pure build because unilateral control cannot be obtained via transactions.
options.B: Equity alliance governance with small stake and minimal operational coordination.
options.C: Non‑equity alliance governance with weaker ties and easy termination.
options.D: Acquisition governance with majority control and hierarchical integration.

2yr-15.explanation: Unilateral control is achieved through acquisition (majority control), not a 50–50 JV that requires shared governance.

2yr-15.stem: In Chapter 9 terms, the JV is most clearly a ‘borrow’ pathway because:

options.A: It eliminates all dependence by making both firms fully independent quickly in practice.
options.B: It equals build because the JV is an internal unit of one partner only.
options.C: It provides access to complementary resources without full acquisition integration in practice.
options.D: It equals buy because a 50–50 JV implies majority control automatically in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: Borrow includes JVs: deeper than contracts, less than acquisition; access to resources comes without full ownership integration.

2yr-15.stem: In build‑borrow‑buy, a key reason to avoid BUY and choose the JV BORROW path is:

options.A: Acquisitions always reduce regulatory scrutiny relative to alliances in practice at scale.
options.B: Integration risk and cultural mismatch can destroy value when absorbing a partner fully.
options.C: Acquisitions always increase flexibility because ownership allows exit easily in practice.
options.D: Acquisitions always reduce integration risk because systems unify immediately in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: Acquisitions carry integration risk and cultural mismatch; the JV can share risk and avoid full integration burdens, though it adds its own governance costs.

2yr-15.stem: In the three-phase alliance management view, the FIRST phase focuses most on:

options.A: Partner selection and alliance formation to match complementarity and incentives.
options.B: Exit planning and divestiture design to unwind the alliance efficiently.
options.C: Integration planning for acquisition because alliance always precedes buy.
options.D: Post‑formation monitoring and conflict resolution after operations start.

2yr-15.explanation: Alliance management begins with partner selection/formation: fit, complementarity, incentives, and clear scope are established early.

2yr-15.stem: In the ‘how alliances work’ logic, relation‑specific investments in this JV would most plausibly include:

options.A: Purely public marketing announcements with no operational or technical change.
options.B: Dedicated interfaces and co-developed architecture that have limited value outside the partnership.
options.C: One-time spot purchases of software tools that require no coordination.
options.D: General-purpose training that increases employee mobility across any employer in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: Relation-specific investments are tailored to the partnership and hard to redeploy elsewhere; they increase mutual commitment.

2yr-15.stem: Interfirm trust is most likely to erode first when:

options.A: Joint routines create transparency in progress and issue resolution over time.
options.B: Governance defines decision rights and escalation paths clearly from the start.
options.C: One party withholds critical information while still demanding partner investment.
options.D: Both parties make relation-specific investments that raise mutual switching costs.

2yr-15.explanation: Withholding information while demanding investment triggers opportunism perceptions; trust is reinforced by transparency, routines, and mutual commitments.

2yr-15.stem: Knowledge-sharing routines in this JV are best understood as:

options.A: Public roadmaps that substitute for technical integration work in practice.
options.B: Contract clauses that eliminate the need for day-to-day collaboration.
options.C: Repeated processes for transfer and joint problem solving, not one-off meetings.
options.D: Ownership stakes that automatically transfer knowledge without interaction in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: Knowledge-sharing routines are repeated processes that enable learning and resource recombination; they are not automatic outcomes of ownership or contracts.

2yr-15.stem: Rivian–VW forming a 50–50 joint venture is best classified as which alliance governance mechanism?

options.A: Acquisition governance using majority control and full hierarchical integration in practice.
options.B: Joint venture governance using a jointly owned entity with shared control rights.
options.C: Non‑equity alliance governance using only short contracts and easy termination.
options.D: Equity alliance governance using a minority stake without creating a new entity.

2yr-15.explanation: A 50–50 jointly owned entity is the definition of a joint venture governance mechanism, the strongest alliance tie short of acquisition.

2yr-15.stem: The SECOND phase of alliance management is best described as:

options.A: Alliance design and governance: allocating decision rights, control, and safeguards.
options.B: Alliance marketing: building brand awareness of the partnership.
options.C: Alliance expansion: merging firms fully into a single hierarchy.
options.D: Alliance termination and divestiture: allocating breakup fees and liabilities.

2yr-15.explanation: Phase 2 is design/governance—structuring contracts, control rights, governance bodies, IP boundaries, and escalation paths.

2yr-15.stem: The THIRD phase of alliance management most directly concerns:

options.A: Governance choice: deciding whether the JV should exist in the first place.
options.B: Integration planning: merging accounting and HR systems into one hierarchy.
options.C: Post‑formation management: execution, learning, conflict handling, and adaptation in practice.
options.D: Partner selection: screening candidates using only financial metrics in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: Post‑formation management includes learning routines, monitoring, conflict resolution, and adapting governance as conditions change.

2yr-15.stem: The most precise definition of an equity alliance (not a JV) is:

options.A: A jointly owned operating company that coordinates shared production in practice.
options.B: A pure contract with no ownership and easy exit and weak ties.
options.C: A full acquisition with unilateral control and integrated hierarchy in practice.
options.D: Minority ownership stake that strengthens ties without creating a new entity.

2yr-15.explanation: Equity alliances involve a minority ownership stake without forming a separate jointly owned operating entity (which would be a JV).

2yr-15.stem: The primary JV advantage over a non‑equity alliance in this case is:

options.A: Higher exit flexibility because JVs dissolve faster than contracts.
options.B: Less need for trust because ownership replaces routines automatically.
options.C: Lower coordination cost because shared entities eliminate conflict.
options.D: Stronger commitment and closeness that supports deep capability sharing.

2yr-15.explanation: JVs create stronger ties and closeness for deep sharing, but they reduce flexibility and can increase coordination burdens; trust/routines still matter.

2yr-15.stem: Which governance adjustment best fits a JV struggling with slow decision making?

options.A: Clarify decision rights and escalation rules without immediately dissolving the JV.
options.B: Shorten the contract to weekly renewals so partners can switch constantly.
options.C: Convert instantly into full acquisition regardless of integration feasibility.
options.D: Increase secrecy and reduce meetings so fewer issues reach top management.

2yr-15.explanation: Many JV problems are governance design issues: clarifying decision rights, escalation, and interfaces can improve speed without drastic moves.

2yr-15.stem: Which governance choice best reduces weak-tie risk relative to a pure contract?

options.A: Pure licensing because licensors always share capabilities deeply.
options.B: JV governance because it increases commitment and shared decision rights.
options.C: Spot contracting because switching often strengthens ties over time.
options.D: No alliance because weak ties disappear when collaboration is avoided.

2yr-15.explanation: JVs are deeper governance forms than contracts, strengthening ties and commitment (though at higher cost and lower flexibility).

2yr-15.stem: Which post‑formation metric best signals improvement in alliance management capability?

options.A: Faster conflict resolution cycles with sustained technical milestones delivery.
options.B: More partner meetings even when decisions remain slow and unresolved.
options.C: More press mentions and keynote announcements with limited technical output.
options.D: Higher executive bonuses regardless of alliance performance outcomes.

2yr-15.explanation: Capability shows up in execution: resolving conflicts faster while hitting milestones; publicity or meeting volume is not a reliable metric.

2yr-15.stem: Which statement best captures why JVs can be required by institutional settings?

options.A: Some jurisdictions or sectors prefer shared local entities for risk and compliance reasons.
options.B: JVs are required because equity alliances are illegal in most markets globally.
options.C: JVs are required because non-equity contracts cannot exist for technology in practice.
options.D: JVs are required because acquisitions are never permitted by regulators in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: Sometimes a JV is used to satisfy local requirements, risk sharing, or compliance constraints; not because other forms are universally illegal.

2yr-15.stem: Which statement best characterises ‘closeness’ in the build‑borrow‑buy logic?

options.A: How geographically close the firms’ headquarters are for travel convenience in practice.
options.B: How similar the firms’ marketing messages are for brand alignment in practice.
options.C: How long the press cycle lasts after announcing the partnership publicly.
options.D: How deep and continuous the interaction must be to access and combine resources.

2yr-15.explanation: Closeness refers to the needed depth of interaction with a partner to access and combine resources, not physical proximity or publicity.

2yr-15.stem: Which statement is the hardest trap in JV governance for executives?

options.A: Assuming shared ownership alone substitutes for trust, routines, and clear decision rights.
options.B: Assuming alliances can never influence competitive advantage in practice at scale.
options.C: Assuming non-equity contracts are always stronger ties than equity alliances.
options.D: Assuming acquisitions are always slower than alliances in dynamic markets.

2yr-15.explanation: Ownership does not remove the need for governance design; decision rights, routines, and trust remain central to alliance success.

2yr-15.stem: A classic reason firms pursue acquisitions instead of alliances is to obtain:

options.A: Higher exit flexibility while preserving weak ties and low commitment levels.
options.B: Guaranteed trust because ownership substitutes for governance routines fully.
options.C: Guaranteed antitrust approval because acquisitions are easier to justify.
options.D: Residual control rights and unilateral decision authority over critical assets.

2yr-15.explanation: Acquisitions provide residual control rights and unilateral authority; they do not guarantee trust or approval.

2yr-15.stem: A federal judge halting the merger primarily raises which Chapter‑9 downside category?

options.A: Experience-curve failure that increases unit costs in internal manufacturing.
options.B: Regulatory and antitrust constraint that can prevent value capture entirely.
options.C: Industry life-cycle mismatch that forces entry into decline stage markets.
options.D: Complement failure that reduces differentiation value drivers in products.

2yr-15.explanation: Even if synergy exists, antitrust constraints can block the deal, preventing any competitive advantage from being realised.

2yr-15.stem: A hard-to-guess reason antitrust can reduce the expected advantage even if deal closes is:

options.A: Antitrust ensures no layoffs, which automatically increases margins at scale in practice.
options.B: Antitrust reduces integration cost because regulators provide free consultants in practice.
options.C: Antitrust always increases synergies because it forces firms to integrate faster.
options.D: Remedies like store divestitures can remove the overlap synergies that justified the deal.

2yr-15.explanation: Divestitures can remove the very assets and overlaps needed for synergies, reducing net value even if a deal proceeds under conditions.

2yr-15.stem: A high-probability reason the merger could have produced a diversification discount rather than premium is:

options.A: Unrelated diversification always creates premium, so discount is impossible.
options.B: Mergers always create premium because market share increases automatically.
options.C: Complexity cost and forced divestitures reduce net synergies below expectation.
options.D: Horizontal integration eliminates coordination costs and reduces complexity.

2yr-15.explanation: Complexity and regulatory remedies can reduce net value; discounts occur when costs exceed synergies.

2yr-15.stem: A non‑intuitive pro of alliances over acquisitions in contested markets is:

options.A: They eliminate the need for trust because partners can litigate easily.
options.B: They eliminate coordination cost because no joint work is required in practice.
options.C: They guarantee monopoly power because firms jointly set prices immediately in practice.
options.D: They can deliver partial benefits without triggering the same level of concentration risk.

2yr-15.explanation: Alliances can provide some scale or capability access with lower concentration; they still require coordination and trust to work.

2yr-15.stem: A non‑intuitive reason M&A fails to create advantage even when strategic fit seems strong is:

options.A: Post‑merger integration costs and culture clash can exceed synergy gains.
options.B: Regulatory review always eliminates integration costs through compliance guidance.
options.C: Acquirers never overpay because markets perfectly price targets in all cases.
options.D: Synergies always appear immediately because scale is instantaneous in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: Integration costs, culture clash, and implementation frictions often exceed expected synergies; overpayment is common and delays are real.

2yr-15.stem: A tough implication of a blocked merger is that the expected advantage fails because:

options.A: The rival response is always stronger than any horizontal scale advantage.
options.B: The pathway is infeasible regardless of internal integration capability.
options.C: Five forces become irrelevant when judges intervene in market structures.
options.D: The firm’s VRIO resources become less valuable in all markets instantly.

2yr-15.explanation: If regulators block the deal, the strategy cannot be implemented; feasibility constraints dominate internal capability considerations.

2yr-15.stem: If Kroger had instead chosen a strategic alliance for joint purchasing, the most Chapter‑9‑consistent advantage would be:

options.A: Guarantee learning because alliances automatically transfer capabilities in practice at scale.
options.B: Guarantee cost savings because contracts specify all future efficiency outcomes.
options.C: Access scale benefits with less integration burden and potentially lower antitrust exposure.
options.D: Guarantee elimination of rivalry because alliances remove competition by default.

2yr-15.explanation: Alliances can access some benefits with lower integration burden; they do not eliminate rivalry by default and cannot guarantee outcomes via complete contracting.

2yr-15.stem: If integration capability is low, the build‑borrow‑buy framework implies that BUY is:

options.A: High risk and may require revisiting borrow or build options instead.
options.B: Mandatory because the only alternative is divestiture in most cases.
options.C: Lower risk because integration capability improves after deal close.
options.D: Automatically superior because acquisition eliminates need for capability in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: Poor integration capability is a major warning sign; the framework suggests revisiting less costly pathways if integration is unlikely to succeed.

2yr-15.stem: If the deal fails, Chapter 9 would classify a ‘plan B’ of joint procurement without merger as:

options.A: Buy pathway because any joint activity implies control transfer.
options.B: Build pathway because procurement scale is always created internally.
options.C: Divest pathway because alliances are retrenchment strategies only in practice.
options.D: Borrow pathway using contractual or alliance governance to access scale benefits.

2yr-15.explanation: Joint procurement without merger is a BORROW approach—contractual collaboration or alliance—rather than build or buy.

2yr-15.stem: If the merger reduced consumer choice and increased prices, this is best described as:

options.A: Unilateral competitive effects consistent with antitrust concerns in horizontal mergers.
options.B: Experience curve advantage consistent with lower learning costs over time.
options.C: Vertical foreclosure consistent with backward integration into suppliers.
options.D: Platform lock-in consistent with cross-side network effects in ecosystems.

2yr-15.explanation: Horizontal mergers can create unilateral effects (less competition), the central antitrust concern in such deals.

2yr-15.stem: In Chapter 9, which statement is most accurate about ‘synergy’?

options.A: Synergy exists whenever market share rises after deal announcement in practice.
options.B: Synergy exists only when combined value exceeds coordination and integration costs.
options.C: Synergy exists whenever the purchase price is lower than the target’s revenue.
options.D: Synergy exists whenever executives announce cost savings in public documents.

2yr-15.explanation: Synergy is net of integration costs. Announced savings or market share changes do not prove synergy.

2yr-15.stem: In horizontal integration, one of the most likely disadvantages is:

options.A: Reduced rivalry always increases consumer welfare and guarantees approval.
options.B: Reduced rivalry always increases innovation and thus lowers prices over time.
options.C: Reduced competitive intensity can invite regulatory scrutiny and forced divestitures.
options.D: Reduced rivalry eliminates substitutes, making industry structure irrelevant in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: Horizontal consolidation can reduce competition, triggering scrutiny and remedies like divestitures, which can undercut anticipated synergies.

2yr-15.stem: Kroger–Albertsons is best classified under Chapter 9 as what type of integration?

options.A: Horizontal integration attempting to combine direct competitors in the same stage.
options.B: Unrelated diversification attempting to enter a distinct industry entirely.
options.C: Backward vertical integration attempting to internalise upstream suppliers in practice.
options.D: Forward vertical integration attempting to internalise downstream retailers in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: The deal combines direct competitors at the same value-chain stage: horizontal integration.

2yr-15.stem: The most precise disadvantage of horizontal integration versus organic growth is:

options.A: Higher flexibility because owned assets can be unwound instantly without cost.
options.B: Lower risk of integration because acquisitions are always smoother than building.
options.C: Higher risk of antitrust constraint and integration burden along with premium paid.
options.D: Lower fixed cost because acquisitions eliminate capital expenditure needs in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: Horizontal acquisitions raise integration burden, antitrust risk, and often require a premium; they are not inherently more flexible or lower capex.

2yr-15.stem: The most precise distinction between a merger and an acquisition is:

options.A: Acquisition involves one firm purchasing controlling interest; merger combines firms into a single entity.
options.B: Merger implies minority ownership; acquisition implies shared 50–50 control in practice at scale.
options.C: Merger always involves cash payment; acquisition always involves stock payment in practice.
options.D: Merger is an alliance form; acquisition is a non-equity contract governance in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: An acquisition is the purchase of control; a merger combines firms into one entity. Payment forms vary.

2yr-15.stem: Which acquisition motive is most consistent with an attempt to reduce rivalry in the same market?

options.A: Market entry via JV to share risk without combining competing assets fully.
options.B: Horizontal integration to consolidate competitors and potentially increase market power.
options.C: Backward integration to control upstream inputs and secure supply stability.
options.D: Capability learning via non-equity alliance with limited commitment and flexibility.

2yr-15.explanation: Horizontal integration is a classic motive to reduce rivalry and increase market power—though it increases antitrust risk.

2yr-15.stem: Which factor most directly increases the risk of ‘overpayment’ in acquisitions?

options.A: Strong culture fit that eliminates integration costs and reduces premiums.
options.B: Regulatory scrutiny that forces lower prices and guarantees value in practice.
options.C: Competitive bidding and managerial optimism that inflates acquisition premiums in practice.
options.D: Low interest rates that reduce debt cost and therefore remove risk entirely.

2yr-15.explanation: Competitive bidding and managerial hubris can drive premiums beyond achievable synergy, producing value destruction even if strategic fit exists.

2yr-15.stem: Which metric is most diagnostic of whether the merger would create advantage, after controlling for announcement effects?

options.A: CEO confidence statements about long-term vision and stakeholder benefits in practice.
options.B: One-day abnormal return around announcement as a complete measure of synergy.
options.C: Sustained operating-margin improvement net of integration costs and divestiture impacts.
options.D: Number of news articles and social media mentions generated by the deal.

2yr-15.explanation: Long-run performance net of integration costs is diagnostic; short-run abnormal returns and publicity are noisy and incomplete.

2yr-15.stem: Which post-merger integration activity is most central to capturing cost synergies in a grocery merger?

options.A: Systems and process integration across procurement, logistics, and store operations.
options.B: Launching unrelated new products to diversify away from grocery competition.
options.C: Rewriting mission statements and values statements without operational changes.
options.D: Replacing all frontline staff immediately to signal cultural transformation.

2yr-15.explanation: Cost synergies depend on integrating systems and processes (procurement, logistics, shared services). Symbolic changes alone do not capture synergy.

2yr-15.stem: Which rationale best matches Kroger’s likely motive if it claimed scale efficiencies to compete better?

options.A: Blue-ocean value innovation to create uncontested demand outside groceries in practice.
options.B: Backward integration to internalise farming inputs and reduce supplier power in practice.
options.C: Unrelated diversification to stabilise cash flows across sectors in practice at scale.
options.D: Economies of scale and scope in procurement and logistics to lower unit costs.

2yr-15.explanation: Horizontal consolidation often targets scale efficiencies in purchasing, distribution, and shared services—core acquisition motives in Chapter 9.

2yr-15.stem: Which statement best captures why acquisitions do not automatically create competitive advantage?

options.A: All acquisitions succeed because ownership resolves contracting hazards fully in practice.
options.B: Deals succeed whenever the target is a competitor in the same industry stage.
options.C: Many deals fail because integration and incentive alignment are hard to execute.
options.D: Deals succeed whenever cost synergies are mentioned in investor presentations in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: Competitive advantage requires successful execution; integration, incentives, culture, and systems are difficult and can destroy expected value.

2yr-15.stem: Which statement best differentiates an alliance from an acquisition in governance terms?

options.A: Alliance eliminates opportunism fully; acquisition increases opportunism always in practice.
options.B: Alliance is only for marketing; acquisition is only for technology transfers.
options.C: Alliance shares some decision rights while keeping firms independent; acquisition transfers control.
options.D: Alliance transfers majority control immediately; acquisition keeps firms independent in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: Governance difference: control and residual rights. Alliances keep firms independent with shared governance; acquisitions transfer control.

2yr-15.stem: Which statement best matches ‘acquisition premium’ and its relevance to value creation?

options.A: Premium guarantees advantage because it signals confidence and commitment in practice at scale.
options.B: Premium must be justified by synergies net of integration costs, or value is destroyed.
options.C: Premium is always recouped because cost savings are immediate at scale in practice.
options.D: Premium is irrelevant because market prices never reflect synergy expectations in practice.

2yr-15.explanation: Paying a premium requires corresponding net synergies; otherwise acquirers overpay and destroy shareholder value.

2yr-15.stem: Which statement is the hardest trap in M&A evaluation for executives?

options.A: Assuming culture fit matters only in unrelated diversification, not in mergers.
options.B: Assuming integration costs are always negative and therefore should be excluded.
options.C: Confusing projected gross synergies with net synergies after integration and remedies.
options.D: Assuming antitrust cannot matter because firms can litigate indefinitely.

2yr-15.explanation: Many M&As fail because executives focus on gross synergies and underweight integration costs, cultural friction, and regulatory remedies.

2yr-17.stem: A core design trade-off in building an ambidextrous organization is balancing:

options.A: Cost discipline via tighter controls with creativity via looser structures and autonomy.
options.B: Geographic scope with horizontal diversification across unrelated industries in practice.
options.C: Supplier power with buyer power through shifts in market structure forces.
options.D: Learning curves with experience curves through scale in production volumes.

2yr-17.explanation: Ambidexterity requires both cost control and creativity; design must balance both.

2yr-17.stem: A functional structure is best characterized by organizing employees primarily by:

options.A: Geographic regions such as EMEA, APAC, and North America regions.
options.B: Domain expertise such as R&D, marketing, finance, and operations functions.
options.C: Product lines such as Search, YouTube, and Cloud as distinct SBUs.
options.D: Customer segments such as enterprise, consumer, and public sector segments.

2yr-17.explanation: Functional structures group employees into specialized functional areas by domain expertise.

2yr-17.stem: A matrix structure is best defined as:

options.A: A pure functional design where all decisions are centralized at headquarters.
options.B: A pure divisional design where functions disappear into SBUs completely.
options.C: A simple design where the founder remains the only strategic decision maker.
options.D: A hybrid of functional and M-form elements creating dual lines of authority.

2yr-17.explanation: the material defines matrix as a mixture of M‑form and functional, often producing dual reporting.

2yr-17.stem: A non-intuitive risk of pushing ‘exploration-only’ for DeepMind is that it may:

options.A: Eliminate organizational inertia because exploration prevents success lock-in.
options.B: Undermine exploitation routines needed to translate research into reliable products.
options.C: Reduce the need for structure because creativity thrives without coordination.
options.D: Guarantee faster value capture because exploration always yields monetization.

2yr-17.explanation: Ambidexterity is needed because exploration alone can weaken exploitation routines that deliver reliability, scale, and capture value.

2yr-17.stem: A plausible downside of making OKRs fully public inside teams is that it can:

options.A: Eliminate the need for culture because numbers fully replace shared values.
options.B: Reduce internal conflict because transparency guarantees perfect alignment in practice.
options.C: Make budgets unnecessary because outcomes are always sufficient for control.
options.D: Shift effort toward measurable targets while crowding out harder-to-measure learning.

2yr-17.explanation: Output metrics can bias effort toward measurable outcomes; complementing controls and culture is often needed for learning and long-horizon work.

2yr-17.stem: A ‘tall hierarchy’ combined with centralized decision authority is most consistent with:

options.A: An organic organization suited to mutual adjustment and decentralized learning.
options.B: A simple structure suited to founder-led rapid pivots without formal systems.
options.C: A matrix structure suited to dual reporting lines and shared program leadership.
options.D: A mechanistic organization suited to predictable outcomes and tight coordination.

2yr-17.explanation: Mechanistic forms emphasize specialization, formalization, and centralized control within a tall hierarchy.

2yr-17.stem: Budgets used by corporate HQ to allocate funds before projects begin are a canonical example of:

options.A: Matrix controls that rely on dual reporting lines to enforce compliance.
options.B: Output controls that guide behavior only through end results and metrics.
options.C: Cultural controls that rely on values and norms rather than formal systems.
options.D: Input controls that direct behavior ex ante through resource constraints.

2yr-17.explanation: Budgets are designed before action and shape decisions ex ante, fitting input controls.

2yr-17.stem: If AI researchers report both to a functional head and a program lead, the most likely new problem is:

options.A: Automatic reduction of inertia because dual reporting prevents resistance in practice.
options.B: Role conflict from dual reporting lines that raises coordination and bargaining costs.
options.C: Loss of specialization because functions are removed and jobs are generalized.
options.D: Elimination of hierarchy because dual reporting implies a flat organization.

2yr-17.explanation: Dual reporting improves integration but often creates role conflict and negotiation overhead.

2yr-17.stem: If Alphabet creates a distinct unit for frontier AI while maintaining strong product interfaces, the best label is:

options.A: A pure M-form shift that turns every product area into an independent SBU.
options.B: A pure organic shift that eliminates hierarchy and formal procedures entirely.
options.C: A structural differentiation that supports exploration while coordinating exploitation in practice.
options.D: A pure mechanistic shift that eliminates autonomy and increases centralization in practice.

2yr-17.explanation: Separate units can support exploration while interfaces maintain coordination with exploitation.

2yr-17.stem: If Alphabet uses OKRs with public team goals to create peer pressure, this mechanism most closely resembles:

options.A: A structural redesign that replaces hierarchy with self-managed holacracy.
options.B: An input control system that specifies detailed procedures before work begins.
options.C: A cultural artifact that substitutes fully for measurement and feedback loops.
options.D: An output control system that specifies outcomes while leaving methods flexible.

2yr-17.explanation: OKRs define objectives and measurable results (outcomes); that aligns with output controls rather than SOP-driven input controls.

2yr-17.stem: If Alphabet wants ‘moonshots’ to have P&L accountability while remaining distinct, the organizational form described is closest to:

options.A: The matrix structure with project-based authority overriding divisional lines.
options.B: The multidivisional (M-form) structure with distinct SBUs and profit responsibility.
options.C: The simple structure with founder centralization and minimal formal systems.
options.D: The functional structure with one P&L and grouping by domain expertise.

2yr-17.explanation: M‑form consists of multiple SBUs, each with profit-and-loss responsibility, coordinated by corporate HQ.

2yr-17.stem: If DeepMind engineers complain ‘R&D never talks to product’ in a functional structure, the cleanest the material diagnosis is:

options.A: Too many two-boss conflicts as a classic matrix-structure drawback.
options.B: Too little specialization as a classic simple-structure drawback.
options.C: Weak cross-functional communication channels as a classic functional-structure drawback.
options.D: Too much divisional autonomy as a classic M-form-structure drawback.

2yr-17.explanation: Functional structures can create strong within-function ties but weak links across functions, causing handoff and coordination failures.

2yr-17.stem: If a capability is highly tradable but requires low closeness, the least costly organizational response is often:

options.A: An M-form redesign because low closeness requires P&L units for each capability.
options.B: A simple structure redesign because low closeness requires founder centralization.
options.C: A non-equity interface with clear contracts rather than deep structural integration.
options.D: A matrix redesign with dual reporting because low closeness implies two bosses.

2yr-17.explanation: When closeness needs are low, coordination can often be handled through lighter interfaces rather than heavy structural changes.

2yr-17.stem: In organizational design terms, Alphabet’s creation of ‘Google DeepMind’ is primarily an intervention in:

options.A: Industry structure to reduce rivalry and raise entry barriers through scale.
options.B: Organizational design to realign structure and processes with a strategic priority.
options.C: Business-level strategy to switch from differentiation to cost leadership quickly.
options.D: Corporate governance to realign principals and agents through board composition.

2yr-17.explanation: A reorg is an organizational design move—reconfiguring structure/process interfaces so strategy can be executed; it is not chiefly governance or industry structure.

2yr-17.stem: In organizational design, a simple structure is most accurately described as one in which:

options.A: The founder makes key strategic decisions while also running daily operations.
options.B: Employees are grouped by domain expertise into specialized departments.
options.C: Teams report to both functional heads and program managers concurrently.
options.D: Distinct SBUs each have P&L responsibility led by divisional CEOs.

2yr-17.explanation: Simple structures concentrate authority and daily operations in the founder/CEO.

2yr-17.stem: In organizational design, ambidexterity requires balancing exploitation with exploration, where exploitation means:

options.A: Applying current knowledge to improve short-run performance and execution quality.
options.B: Outsourcing innovation entirely so the firm focuses on cost discipline.
options.C: Replacing hierarchy with markets so employees self-organize around tasks.
options.D: Searching for new knowledge to improve future performance and new options.

2yr-17.explanation: Exploitation is short-run performance improvement using existing knowledge; exploration is searching for new knowledge for future performance.

2yr-17.stem: In organizational design, the ‘goal’ of organizational design is best phrased as:

options.A: Designing an organization that permanently locks in success by resisting change.
options.B: Designing an organization that maximizes rivalry reduction through consolidation.
options.C: Designing an organization that translates chosen strategy into realized strategy effectively.
options.D: Designing an organization that replaces leadership with automated decision rules.

2yr-17.explanation: Organizational design aims to translate chosen strategy into realized strategy via structure, culture, and control.

2yr-17.stem: In the strategy–structure evolution described in the material, growth most predictably pushes firms from functional structure toward:

options.A: A purely mechanistic structure to maximize formalization and control.
options.B: A purely organic structure to remove hierarchy and formal procedures.
options.C: A simple structure to concentrate authority back in the founder’s hands.
options.D: An M-form to handle multiple SBUs with profit-and-loss responsibility.

2yr-17.explanation: As firms grow in size and complexity, structure tends to progress from functional to multidivisional (M‑form), and sometimes to matrix.

2yr-17.stem: The best the material remedy for poor cross-functional linkage in a functional structure is to create:

options.A: Cross-functional teams with temporary project authority and dual reporting.
options.B: More centralization so the CEO makes all integration decisions personally.
options.C: More specialization within functions to deepen expertise and reduce interaction.
options.D: Higher formalization to replace dialogue with standard operating procedures.

2yr-17.explanation: Cross-functional teams can overcome weak links across departments; they often entail dual reporting and coordination needs.

2yr-17.stem: The four building blocks of organizational structure in the material are:

options.A: Diversification, integration, globalization, and ambidexterity as core design levers.
options.B: Differentiation, cost drivers, complements, and switching costs as core design levers.
options.C: Specialization, formalization, centralization, and hierarchy as core design levers.
options.D: Market power, entry barriers, substitutes, and rivalry as core design levers.

2yr-17.explanation: the material defines structure via specialization, formalization, centralization, and hierarchy.

2yr-17.stem: The four-step path to organizational inertia begins with which condition?

options.A: Immediate decentralization of decisions that forces flexibility and reinvention in practice.
options.B: Sudden collapse in financial metrics that triggers rapid restructuring efforts in practice.
options.C: Mastery of and fit with the current environment that becomes hard to question.
options.D: Open innovation boundaries that make the firm permeable to external ideas.

2yr-17.explanation: Exhibit 11.2 describes the inertia path as: (1) mastery/fit → (2) success measured financially → (3) structures/metrics → (4) inertia.

2yr-17.stem: The most precise reason ‘structure follows strategy’ matters for Google DeepMind is that:

options.A: Strategy is always correct, so structure merely signals commitment to markets.
options.B: Structure replaces leadership judgment, so managers need not choose trade-offs.
options.C: Execution requires design that translates formulated strategy into realized actions.
options.D: Structure determines industry forces, so firms can redesign rivalry at will.

2yr-17.explanation: Organizational design is a translation mechanism from strategy to realized actions.

2yr-17.stem: When external PESTEL shocks pierce a tightly coupled strategy–structure system, the material predicts the firm risks:

options.A: Higher efficiency because inertia protects the firm from noisy environments in practice.
options.B: Lower need for redesign because structure becomes more stable under pressure.
options.C: Breakdown of the current design leading to failure unless it reboots and adapts.
options.D: Automatic improvement because shocks always trigger productive learning in practice at scale.

2yr-17.explanation: External/internal shifts can break apart a tightly coupled system; avoiding failure requires adaptive redesign (Option B cycle).

2yr-17.stem: Which choice is NOT a component of organizational design as defined in the material?

options.A: Structure, leadership, and diversification as the three levers leaders manipulate.
options.B: Structure, culture, and control as the three levers leaders can manipulate.
options.C: Structure, culture, and control as a translation device for execution.
options.D: Structure, culture, and control as an integrated implementation architecture.

2yr-17.explanation: the material defines organizational design’s components as structure, culture, and control—not diversification.

2yr-17.stem: Which statement is most faithful to the the material warning about strategy often following structure?

options.A: Managers choose strategy first and then freely redesign structure without friction.
options.B: Managers focus on industry forces only because internal design has little effect.
options.C: Managers pursue only blue oceans because ambidexterity solves all trade-offs.
options.D: Managers may restrict strategy choices to avoid changing power and resource allocation.

2yr-17.explanation: Inertia and politics can cause managers to consider only strategies that fit existing structures rather than redesigning.

2yr-17.stem: A common mistake when diagnosing ‘culture problems’ is to treat them as purely:

options.A: Structure issues rather than values and norms shaping everyday behavior.
options.B: Messaging issues rather than reinforcement through hiring and reward systems.
options.C: Market issues rather than internal coordination and incentive alignment issues.
options.D: Strategy issues rather than implementation architecture and control choices.

2yr-17.explanation: Culture problems are rarely fixed by messaging alone; reinforcement mechanisms matter.

2yr-17.stem: A culture change effort is most likely to fail if Netflix changes slogans but does NOT change:

options.A: Selection, socialization, and reward systems that reinforce daily behavior patterns.
options.B: Cost drivers, because culture depends only on economies of scale and learning.
options.C: Geographic scope, because culture cannot change within one national context.
options.D: Industry structure, because culture shifts require changing rivalry and entry barriers.

2yr-17.explanation: Culture is reinforced by hiring, training, promotion, and reward systems; slogans without reinforcement rarely stick.

2yr-17.stem: A non-intuitive risk of strong culture is that it can produce:

options.A: Groupthink where dissent is suppressed and assumptions go unchallenged over time.
options.B: Perfect adaptation because strong norms always increase diversity of thought.
options.C: Lower inertia because strong culture prevents success lock-in always.
options.D: Automatic innovation because strong values eliminate need for exploration.

2yr-17.explanation: Strong, cohesive cultures can lead to groupthink, especially when diversity is low and dissent is punished.

2yr-17.stem: A robust indicator that culture is changing is that new hires begin to:

options.A: Report to different bosses because the organizational chart changed immediately.
options.B: Face different competitors because industry rivalry has structurally transformed.
options.C: Display different day-to-day norms because selection and socialization have shifted.
options.D: Adopt different cost drivers because learning curves improved quickly.

2yr-17.explanation: Culture change shows up in everyday norms and behaviors, especially in hiring, onboarding, and promotion patterns.

2yr-17.stem: A spending cap is classified as input control because it is:

options.A: A structural device that reallocates reporting relationships among teams.
options.B: An artifact expressing values but leaving all decisions unconstrained.
options.C: Considered before the value-creating activity and constrains choices ex ante.
options.D: Considered after the activity and only evaluates outcomes against benchmarks.

2yr-17.explanation: Input controls are designed prior to decisions and constrain behavior before action is taken.

2yr-17.stem: A subtle drawback of output controls at the corporate level is that they can:

options.A: Reduce the need for structure because charts become irrelevant with targets.
options.B: Eliminate conflict because targets provide complete alignment across divisions in practice.
options.C: Discourage collaboration if units optimize local targets at the expense of shared goals.
options.D: Replace culture because metrics fully dictate what employees should value in practice.

2yr-17.explanation: Outcome controls can discourage collaboration among units when targets create siloed optimization.

2yr-17.stem: If Netflix formalizes approval gates for content spending, it is most directly increasing:

options.A: Organic coordination through mutual adjustment without rules or documents.
options.B: Decentralization through moving decisions closer to frontline creative staff.
options.C: Formalization through codified procedures that reduce discretion in spending choices.
options.D: Specialization through narrower jobs that deepen expertise in content creation.

2yr-17.explanation: Approval gates are codified procedures—formalization—reducing discretion and variability.

2yr-17.stem: If Netflix offers severance to encourage non-fit employees to exit early, it most closely mirrors:

options.A: OKR peer pressure created solely by public stretch goals and dashboards.
options.B: Zappos-style exit incentives reinforcing cultural fit via employee self-selection.
options.C: Matrix escalation routines resolving dual reporting conflicts through committees.
options.D: M-form budgeting allocating corporate capital to SBUs with P&L accountability.

2yr-17.explanation: Exit incentives can reinforce cultural fit by encouraging self-selection, similar to the Zappos example in the material.

2yr-17.stem: If Netflix replaces vague ‘freedom’ language with explicit ‘accountability’ norms, it is primarily redefining:

options.A: Values that define what is considered important and non-negotiable always.
options.B: Norms that shape expected employee behaviors and attitudes in daily work.
options.C: Centralization that moves decision authority upward to top management.
options.D: Specialization that divides tasks into narrow jobs and expert roles.

2yr-17.explanation: Norms define appropriate attitudes/behaviors; values define what matters. The shift is largely normative guidance for behavior.

2yr-17.stem: If Netflix ties bonuses to subscriber retention targets while letting teams choose methods, that is closest to:

options.A: Input controls guiding behavior through SOPs and procedural compliance checks.
options.B: Simple-structure control guiding behavior through direct founder supervision.
options.C: Output controls guiding behavior through results rather than prescribed processes.
options.D: Founder imprinting guiding behavior through the founder’s personal lifestyle.

2yr-17.explanation: Output controls define expected results; the means remain open to teams or individuals.

2yr-17.stem: If Netflix uses senior leaders’ behavior to signal ‘cost discipline’ despite autonomy, that is primarily:

options.A: Structural redesign because leader behavior changes the organizational chart.
options.B: Input control because role modeling substitutes for budgets and policies.
options.C: Cultural leadership through role modeling, reinforcing norms without formal rules.
options.D: Output control because role modeling directly defines measurable results.

2yr-17.explanation: Role modeling is a cultural lever; leaders’ actions signal norms even when rules are not explicit.

2yr-17.stem: If Netflix wants creativity with cost discipline, the most defensible the material approach is to:

options.A: Adopt full mechanistic design so creativity is replaced by predictable SOP outcomes in practice.
options.B: Shift to M-form so each show is an SBU with its own CEO and P&L authority.
options.C: Mix loose autonomy norms with targeted input controls on high-risk spend categories in practice.
options.D: Adopt full organic design so budgets and caps are removed and costs are ignored.

2yr-17.explanation: Balancing trade-offs is central: keep autonomy where it drives creativity while adding targeted controls where predictability and risk management matter.

2yr-17.stem: In organizational design, artifacts are best defined as:

options.A: Input controls such as budgets and SOPs that specify behavior before action.
options.B: Unobservable assumptions that cannot be detected through any external signals.
options.C: Formal reporting lines that specify hierarchy, span of control, and centralization.
options.D: Observable expressions of culture such as documents, rituals, symbols, and stories.

2yr-17.explanation: Artifacts are visible expressions of culture; they signal values and norms.

2yr-17.stem: Introducing spending caps is the clearest example of:

options.A: Output controls that specify results while leaving all means fully flexible.
options.B: Matrix control that relies on dual reporting lines and program authority.
options.C: Input controls that constrain actions ex ante through explicit rules and budgets.
options.D: Cultural control that relies on shared beliefs rather than formal mechanisms.

2yr-17.explanation: Spending caps and budgets are input controls because they shape choices before the activity occurs.

2yr-17.stem: Netflix increasing salary bands while keeping autonomy is an example of combining:

options.A: Only culture because pay structures never influence behavior significantly in practice.
options.B: Only output controls because salary bands are results-based measures always.
options.C: Some input controls with cultural autonomy rather than choosing only one lever.
options.D: Only structure because salary bands change reporting lines and authority.

2yr-17.explanation: Compensation structures can function as controls; firms often mix culture and controls rather than relying on one.

2yr-17.stem: Netflix revising a culture memo is best framed as a change to which organizational design lever?

options.A: Organizational strategy, because memos replace the AFI framework entirely.
options.B: Organizational culture, because the memo encodes shared values and norms.
options.C: Organizational structure, because a memo directly changes reporting lines.
options.D: Industry structure, because cultural language shifts rivalry and entry barriers.

2yr-17.explanation: Culture is the collectively shared values and norms; a culture memo is an artifact expressing and shaping culture.

2yr-17.stem: Netflix’s culture memo is most accurately an artifact that works because it:

options.A: Makes values and norms explicit, influencing selection, socialization, and reward fit.
options.B: Substitutes for structure because no reporting lines are needed in practice.
options.C: Eliminates the need for metrics because text alone directs performance outcomes.
options.D: Replaces hierarchy because artifacts automatically decentralize decision authority in practice.

2yr-17.explanation: Artifacts help encode and communicate culture; they interact with hiring, training, and reward systems, not replace them.

2yr-17.stem: Output controls are especially effective when:

options.A: Collaboration across SBUs is required, because output controls always increase it.
options.B: Outcomes are impossible to measure, so goals must remain fully subjective always.
options.C: Internal factors make the effort–performance link clear enough to set targets fairly.
options.D: Employees have no autonomy, so output controls specify every action step.

2yr-17.explanation: Output controls work well when the relationship between effort and performance is more internally determined and measurable.

2yr-17.stem: Removing ambiguous ‘brilliant jerk’ language is most directly aimed at strengthening:

options.A: Formalization so SOPs specify every creative decision step precisely.
options.B: Norm clarity so behavioral expectations are less contestable across teams.
options.C: Centralization so approvals move upward and autonomy is reduced fully.
options.D: Hierarchy so spans of control expand and managerial layers increase.

2yr-17.explanation: Clarifying cultural language tightens norms; it is not the same as procedural formalization or added hierarchy.

2yr-17.stem: The best the material example of founder imprinting is:

options.A: A founder shaping enduring norms that persist long after departure from leadership.
options.B: A firm adopting cost leadership by outsourcing production to low-cost regions.
options.C: A board selecting an external auditor to monitor financial reporting accuracy.
options.D: A firm entering a foreign market by franchising rather than investing capital.

2yr-17.explanation: Founder imprinting is when founders define and shape culture in ways that persist for decades.

2yr-17.stem: The most precise definition of organizational culture in the material is:

options.A: Formal rules and SOPs that specify each action step for predictable outcomes.
options.B: The set of market forces that determine rivalry and profitability in the industry.
options.C: The organizational chart showing reporting lines and spans of control only.
options.D: Collectively shared values and norms that shape members’ interpretations and actions.

2yr-17.explanation: Culture is shared values and norms; it is distinct from structure (charts) and controls (rules/SOPs).

2yr-17.stem: Which option is NOT a control mechanism emphasized in the material?

options.A: PESTEL controls through political and ecological forces that managers cannot alter.
options.B: Cultural controls through values and norms shaping behavior informally.
options.C: Input controls through budgets and SOPs considered before business decisions.
options.D: Output controls through targets tied to rewards with flexible execution methods.

2yr-17.explanation: PESTEL is external analysis; controls in the material are internal governance mechanisms such as input/output controls and culture-based controls.

2yr-17.stem: Which pair best captures the values–norms distinction?

options.A: Values define industry forces; norms define strategic groups and mobility barriers.
options.B: Values define specialization; norms define centralization and hierarchy levels.
options.C: Values define reporting lines; norms define budgets and input controls always.
options.D: Values define what matters; norms define expected behaviors and attitudes daily.

2yr-17.explanation: Values = what’s important; norms = what behaviors/attitudes are appropriate.

2yr-17.stem: Which statement about artifacts is correct?

options.A: Artifacts are identical to SOPs because they prescribe each action step.
options.B: Artifacts are identical to norms because they directly prescribe attitudes daily.
options.C: Artifacts are visible signals of culture but do not guarantee alignment with behavior.
options.D: Artifacts are identical to values because they define what is important always.

2yr-17.explanation: Artifacts can be symbolic; without reinforcement, they can diverge from actual norms and behaviors.

2yr-17.stem: Which statement is most correct about strong culture and competitive advantage?

options.A: It supports advantage only when accompanied by complete SOP formalization in practice at scale.
options.B: It always supports advantage because strong values guarantee adaptability always in practice at scale.
options.C: It can support advantage when aligned with strategy, but it can also lock in inertia.
options.D: It never supports advantage because culture is soft and cannot shape outcomes in practice.

2yr-17.explanation: Culture can be a source of advantage when aligned, but it can also produce rigidity and groupthink, contributing to inertia.

2yr-17.stem: A balanced scorecard is relevant in the material primarily as an example of:

options.A: A structural form that replaces functional departments with SBUs entirely.
options.B: A make-or-buy framework that allocates activities between firms and markets.
options.C: A strategic control system that broadens measurement beyond single financial metrics.
options.D: A culture artifact that substitutes for reward systems and incentives fully.

2yr-17.explanation: Control systems can include balanced scorecards to avoid overfocus on one metric; the material frames it within control-and-reward systems.

2yr-17.stem: A key difference between input and output controls is that input controls:

options.A: Rely on founder imprinting rather than codified procedures and budgets.
options.B: Require matrix dual reporting so supervisors enforce compliance jointly.
options.C: Specify methods and rules before action, aiming for predictable conversion processes.
options.D: Specify results after action while leaving all methods constrained and fixed.

2yr-17.explanation: Input controls define methods ex ante (budgets, SOPs). Output controls specify expected results and allow discretion in methods.

2yr-17.stem: A key non-intuitive cause of quality failures in a tightly coupled system is that:

options.A: Decentralization always reduces errors because frontline workers know best in practice.
options.B: Organic organizations cannot produce high reliability under any conditions in practice.
options.C: Formal rules prevent deviations because employees always comply perfectly in practice.
options.D: Local workarounds become norms even when formal rules appear adequate on paper.

2yr-17.explanation: Culture and informal norms can override formal rules; workarounds can become ‘the real process’ unless controls and culture reinforce compliance.

2yr-17.stem: A non-intuitive risk of extreme mechanistic controls is that they can:

options.A: Reduce problem reporting if employees fear blame and merely ‘comply’ superficially.
options.B: Eliminate culture risk because procedures fully replace norms and trust.
options.C: Guarantee learning because formalization always increases voice and disclosure.
options.D: Remove inertia because compliance systems constantly force redesign cycles.
